passages.text: Studies have found that genistein can inhibit the differentiation of mononuclear macrophages into osteoclasts by regulating the RANKL/OPG signaling pathway, reduce osteoclast activity, reduce bone resorption, and thus reduce alveolar bone destruction caused by periodontitis. Bhattarai et al.  showed that intraperitoneal injection of genistein (20 mg/kg) every day for 3 consecutive weeks could inhibit LPS-mediated alveolar bone loss and periodontal tissue degradation. The protective effect on alveolar bone is achieved by regulating RANKL. Similarly, through micro-CT analysis, Choi et al.  found that genistein reduced the loss of alveolar bone height and bone volume fraction in rat periodontitis induced by ligation and also prevented changes in trabecular microstructure parameters (trabecular thickness, trabecular separation, bone mineral density, and structural model index), suggesting that genistein may potentially be utilized in the future for the treatment of human periodontitis.

Zhang et al.  found that administration of genistein (20 and 40 mg/kg) can reduce alveolar bone resorption in periodontitis mice induced by silk ligation, which may be related to its bone protection. In addition, Dai et al.  confirmed that genistein reduced osteoclast formation. In the study of mechanism, it was found that genistein could inhibit the expression of RANKL and increase the expression of OPG in periodontal tissue of rats with periodontitis. It could also reduce the levels of Slit homolog 2 (Slit2) and P38 MAPK phosphorylated protein in rats with periodontitis, so as to draw a conclusion. Genistein can reduce periodontal tissue inflammation and alveolar bone resorption in periodontitis rats. The mechanism may be related to the inhibition of Slit2 / P38 MAPK signaling pathway, regulation of RANKL/OPG expression, and inhibition of osteoclast formation.

Interleukin-17 (IL-17) is an important cytokine secreted by Th17, which has the function of stimulating human periodontal ligament cells to express RANKL and promote osteoclast differentiation (Ikeuchi and Moutsopoulos ). Estrogen deficiency leads to a downregulation of genes encoding tight junction proteins in the gingiva, an elevation of IL-17 levels, and an acceleration of alveolar bone resorption. Studies have found that genistein treatment can alleviate the gene levels of IL-17 in ovariectomized experimental periodontitis rats, increase the expression of tight junction proteins, and prevent the absorption of alveolar bone (Liu et al. ).
Genistein Promotes Osteogenic Process

As a safe and effective "phytoestrogen," genistein can promote osteoblast proliferation, differentiation, and mineralized bone formation and inhibit osteoclast bone resorption. There are many molecular mechanisms of anti-osteoporosis. It can selectively bind to estrogen receptor (ER) in vivo and play a role in the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis. The mechanism may be to promote the proliferation, differentiation and mineralization of osteoblasts through PPARgamma, BMP/Smads/Runx2, MAPK/NF-kappaB/AP-1 and other signaling pathways. At the same time, it can inhibit osteoclast bone resorption through NF-kappaB pathway and intracellular calcium signaling pathway (Zheng et al. ). Furthermore, genistein has an anabolic effect on osteoblast MC3T3-E1 in vitro (Sugimoto and Yamaguchi ). Furthermore, numerous studies have demonstrated that genistein possesses the ability to enhance bone regeneration and elevate bone density (Chan et al. ).

As periodontitis progressively worsens, it leads to irreversible damage to the alveolar bone. This pathological change is highlighted by the breakdown of the original balance between osteoclast-driven bone decomposition (bone resorption) and osteoblast-driven bone synthesis (bone formation) (Hienz et al. ). Guo et al. established a rat model of experimental periodontitis with osteoporosis and found that genistein effectively improved the changes in biochemical indexes of bone metabolism caused by estrogen deficiency. The levels of alkaline phosphatase (AKP) and bone gla protein (BGP) were significantly increased, indicating that genistein contributes to bone formation and the maintenance of normal bone calcification and effectively prevents alveolar bone resorption caused by estrogen deficiency in rats with periodontal disease, which can play a role in alternative estrogen therapy (Yang et al. ). Figure 3 is an overview of the mechanism of genistein in the treatment of periodontitis.

Overview of the mechanism of genistein in the treatment of periodontitis. Novel drug delivery systems for genistein, such as nanoparticles, liposomes, polymer micelles, hydrogels, solid dispersions, and microspheres, exhibit exceptional solubility, targeting, and sustained release, overcoming its poor water solubility and enabling effective periodontitis treatment. In periodontitis, genistein potently suppresses inflammatory mediators (IL-1beta, TNF-alpha, etc.), exhibiting anti-inflammatory activity. It also modulates bone metabolism by inhibiting RANKL and enhancing OPG, AKP, and BGP expression, contributing to bone protection. passages.text: Genistein Inhibits Bacterial Process

Periodontal disease is characterized by a mixed bacterial infection that results in inflammatory destruction of the periodontal tissues that support and surround the teeth. The periodontal microbiota comprises a complex dental plaque biofilm ecosystem, where pathogenic bacteria produce virulence factors that allow them to evade host defenses and elicit a detrimental immune response in the host tissues. Periodontal disease arises due to an imbalance or disruption in the normal homeostasis among plaque bacteria, the host immune system, and the environmental conditions present in a healthy state (Harvey ). More than 700 different microorganisms have been isolated from the human oral cavity, including aerobes, facultative anaerobic bacteria, and obligate anaerobic bacteria, as well as other microorganisms such as spirochetes, fungi, archaea, mycoplasma, viruses, and protozoa (Zhang et al. ). Currently, the antibacterial agents frequently employed in the treatment of periodontitis encompass nitroimidazoles, tetracyclines, penicillins, and macrolides; however, these agents are prone to inducing the emergence of drug-resistant strains and may elicit adverse effects, including gastrointestinal disturbances and systemic allergic reactions (Soares et al. ).

Genistein exhibits antibacterial properties, demonstrating its potential as an antimicrobial agent. A study suggested that  Staphylococcus aureus , a medically important pathogen, was found at a high prevalence in non-smoking individuals with aggressive periodontitis. Moreover, a diagnostic utility distinguishing between aggressive and chronic periodontitis sites was found for  P. intermedia ,  S. aureus , and  S. mutans  (Fritschi et al. ). In addition,  S. aureus  is an early-colonizing bacterium of titanium surfaces (Furst et al. ), and a pathogen in periimplantitis (Leonhardt et al. ). A standardized in vitro experiment was conducted to assess the direct impact of genistein on bacterial growth. In bacterial colony-forming unit (CFU) assays, notable decreases in CFU counts were observed for  Staphylococcus aureus  and  Bacillus anthracis  when cultivated in the presence of 100 muM genistein. Additionally, the incorporation of genistein alongside probiotics has the potential to enhance the efficacy of existing antimicrobial treatments utilized in infection management (Hong et al. ). In another study by Guo , the impact of genistein on MRSA (methicillin-resistant  S. aureus )-induced osteomyelitis was examined in male Wistar rats. The results indicated a decrease in pro-inflammatory cytokines, specifically IL-6 and TNF-alpha, as well as a reduction in bacterial growth.

Helicobacter pylori  (Hp) serves as a pathogen for chronic gastritis and gastric ulcer, and recent research has demonstrated that dental plaque functions as a reservoir for this bacterium. Specifically, Hp can be identified within periodontal pockets, with a notably higher detection rate observed in cases of gingival bleeding compared to non-bleeding instances (Maurotto et al. ). One study showed that the risk for positive in the periodontitis test was higher among subjects with Hp infection as compared with those without, while post-eradicated status tended to reduce that risk (Adachi et al. ). A study has demonstrated that genistein possesses potent antibacterial activity in vitro. Exposure to genistein exhibited an inhibitory effect on all staphylococcal strains tested. Furthermore, the growth of Hp was clearly inhibited by genistein (Verdrengh et al. ). Research findings have demonstrated that genistein exerts gastroprotective effects in rats with Hp-induced gastropathy by means of reducing the levels of pro-inflammatory mediators, downregulating the expression of the nuclear receptor NF-kappaB, and mitigating gastric mucosal apoptosis (Siriviriyakul et al. ).

Up to now, there has been a lot of evidence to fully support  Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans ,  Porphyromonas gingivalis , and  Tannerella forsythia  as the key pathogenic bacteria of periodontal disease (Ursu et al. ). These bacterial strains occupy a central position in the development of periodontal disease, especially concerning the degradation of periodontal tissues. However, there is still a lack of research on the interaction between genistein and the above important pathogenic bacteria related to periodontitis, and there are few reports in the relevant scientific literature. Given that genistein is a natural compound with potential antibacterial activity, its inhibitory effect on certain bacteria in vitro experiments suggests that the antibacterial properties of genistein are worthy of further exploration, especially in the intervention strategy for the pathogenesis of periodontitis. Therefore, future research directions can focus on elucidating the specific mechanism of action between genistein and periodontitis pathogens and evaluating its potential as an adjuvant treatment for periodontal disease, thus paving the way for innovative approaches in the prevention and management of periodontal disease.
Clinical Study

A clinical study was conducted on 3956 students (aged 18-22 years) to collect information on dietary factors using a validated dietary history questionnaire. Logistic regression analysis was employed to ascertain the odds ratio and corresponding confidence interval associated with periodontal disease. Smoking, brushing frequency, place of residence, and body mass index were adjusted. The results showed that the intake of foods containing genistein may reduce the possibility of periodontal disease (Tanaka et al. ). Currently, a substantial absence of extensive clinical investigations into genistein's application for periodontitis treatment persists, necessitating additional confirmatory trials to advance its clinical adoption.

In conclusion, genistein exerts therapeutic effects in periodontitis through three key mechanisms: (1) suppressing periodontal soft tissue inflammation, (2) inhibiting osteoclast activity while promoting osteoblast function to reduce alveolar bone resorption, and (3) inhibiting the growth of specific pathogenic bacteria implicated in the disease. Although genistein exhibits a notable therapeutic effect in the treatment of periodontitis, current research on its mechanisms for inhibiting alveolar bone resorption and its antibacterial properties in periodontitis remain limited, necessitating further investigation.
Common Delivery Systems of Genistein

In recent years, genistein has attracted much attention in the field of oral medicine as a potential natural drug. Improving the solubility and bioavailability of genistein has important guiding significance for further exploring other related parameters of its pharmacokinetics, which not only helps us to understand the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion process of genistein in vivo more comprehensively, but also provides a scientific basis for optimizing the design of pharmaceutical preparations, improving drug efficacy, and reducing the risk of adverse reactions in the adjuvant treatment of periodontitis.

With the aim of enhancing the bioavailability of genistein, a variety of strategies have been implemented, among which nanoparticles, liposomes, polymer micelles, hydrogels, solid dispersions, and microspheres are the most widely used. We hope that by optimizing the drug delivery system of genistein, its solubility can be improved and its pharmacological activity may be enhanced, thus showing more excellent efficacy in the protection and treatment of periodontal soft and hard tissues. Nanoparticle

Nanoparticles are solid-state drug-loaded colloidal particles prepared by nanotechnology. The particle size ranges from 10 to 1000 nm, and the drug is encapsulated by dissolution, adsorption, or encapsulation. As a nano-controlled release system, nanoparticles can significantly improve the targeting, bioavailability, and therapeutic effect of drugs and significantly enhance the water solubility, storage stability, and release controllability of drugs. This technology not only reduces the dose of administration, reduces the side effects of drugs, but also opens up an important way for the development and utilization of drugs with poor water solubility (Liu et al. ; Mitchell et al. ).

Tang et al.  prepared genistein nanoparticles using nanoprecipitation technology. In contrast to genistein suspensions, the nanoparticle formulations effectively encapsulate the drug within suitable carrier materials to create novel nanoparticle preparations. These preparations substantially optimize the in vitro dissolution characteristics of genistein, leading to a significant enhancement in its bioavailability. With the aim of achieving targeted drug delivery, Patra et al.  employed nanoprecipitation technology to synthesize nanoparticles encapsulated with genistein. This formulation enhanced the extent to which genistein was internalized by cells, prolonged the duration of drug release, and ultimately resulted in an improvement in its anti-cancer effectiveness. Alam and Akhlaq  formulated nanoparticles encapsulating genistein with the aim of enhancing its bioavailability. The nanoparticles obtained exhibited an average particle size of 123 nm, exhibiting superior drug release characteristics in comparison to conventional dosage forms, while also possessing a high encapsulation efficiency.

A different research team developed MIL-100(Fe) metal-organic framework nanoparticles via a straightforward impregnation technique, aiming to enhance the oral bioavailability of genistein. The resultant formulation exhibited sustained release of genistein over a 3-day period, coupled with an improvement in bioavailability, thereby establishing itself as an effective drug delivery strategy (Botet-Carreras et al. ). Zhang et al.  fabricated genistein-loaded nanoparticles specifically designed for enhanced delivery to target cells. The findings indicated that these nanoparticles exhibited heightened efficacy in inhibiting tumor growth. The results imply that nanoparticles represent promising formulations for the effective delivery of genistein.

Given the limited application potential of genistein in the treatment of periodontal disease due to its poor water solubility and other unfavorable physical properties, it is proposed to utilize solid lipid nanoparticle technology for its encapsulation. The objective is to increase the drug concentration in both plasma and cells, thereby enhancing the bioavailability of genistein. Additionally, this technology is expected to improve the aqueous solution stability and targeting abilities of genistein, ultimately leading to an amplification of its therapeutic efficacy.
Liposome

Liposomes are a special class of vesicles formed by phospholipids. They have a structure similar to that of ordinary vesicles, which can effectively disperse fat-soluble drugs in aqueous media. When the fat-soluble drug is encapsulated by liposomes, it can exhibit excellent characteristics such as targeting, sustained release, and stability and has low toxicity. It is a new and advanced drug delivery system (Large et al. ). The encapsulation of genistein within liposomes can appreciably enhance an array of its physical and chemical properties, such as solubility, stability, and bioavailability, thereby optimizing its therapeutic potential and enhancing its effectiveness in various biomedical applications.

passages.text: Research has proposed a novel microgel oral delivery system, loaded with liposome nanoparticles containing a natural anti-inflammatory compound genistein into alginate microgels, thereby achieving the targeted release of genistein in the colonic region and ameliorating ulcerative colitis symptoms (Yan et al. ). Furthermore, Phan et al.  formulated genistein-encapsulated liposomes and demonstrated their efficacy in enhancing the solubilization and stability of genistein, as well as prolonging its release profile. A research team formulated azolectin-encapsulated genistein liposomes to explore the interplay between genistein and azolectin. These liposomes exhibited heightened in vitro activities, thereby amplifying their antitumoral effects (Lopes de Azambuja et al. ). In a combinatorial or multifunctional approach aimed at treating prostate cancer, a liposomal formulation was developed that incorporated genistein along with celecoxib (Tian et al. ) and plumbagin (Tian et al. ). Studies conducted on this formulation revealed a significant enhancement in its efficacy for addressing prostate cancer. Additionally, in a separate study, phytosomes loaded with genistein were engineered to improve the solubility of the compound. In vivo experiments further demonstrated that these phytosomes exhibited an elevated anti-tumor effect (Komeil et al. ).

In the realm of periodontitis treatment strategies, consideration is given to employing bovine serum albumin for the construction of a long-circulating drug delivery system for genistein liposomes. This approach leverages their multiple advantages, including reduced phagocytosis, sustained release properties, improved stability, and non-toxic nature. Furthermore, by incorporating targeted liposome preparation technology, it is expected that the therapeutic efficacy of genistein in treating periodontitis will be significantly improved, ultimately resulting in more targeted and effective treatment outcomes.
Polymeric Micelle

Polymeric micelles represent a class of self-assembled nanoparticles characterized by a hydrophobic core encapsulated by a hydrophilic shell. As a widely researched nano-drug delivery system, targeted polymeric micelles have demonstrated substantial value in clinical applications owing to their exceptional tissue permeability, which is often attributed to their unique structural features and ability to facilitate the delivery of therapeutic agents to specific sites within the body (Hwang et al. ). The encapsulation of genistein within polymeric micelles can enhance diverse physicochemical properties of the drug, ultimately optimizing its therapeutic efficacy.

Research studies have employed micelle-like nanoparticles as a carrier system for encapsulating genistein, with the aim of enhancing the therapeutic efficacy in the treatment of ocular neovascularization (Kim et al. ). Similarly, Shen et al.  designed mixed micelles encapsulating genistein to overcome its solubility challenges and augment its bioavailability. Their findings revealed a high degree of entrapment efficiency and drug loading capacity. Cheng et al.  formulated micelles containing genistein by utilizing a modified emulsion-evaporation method. In vitro studies conducted on this formulation revealed enhanced solubility and bioavailability of genistein.

In a separate study, Kwon et al.  formulated micelles encapsulating genistein using the solid dispersion technique. Their findings revealed an improved drug loading efficiency and an enhanced release profile for genistein, ultimately resulting in an increased bioavailability. Hou et al.  designed glycyrrhizin-based micelles as a nanocarrier system for genistein, with the objective of augmenting its therapeutic efficacy. In vivo studies have demonstrated the exceptional tolerability and the improved corneal penetration exhibited by the genistein-loaded micelles. Thus, micelles have been identified as an efficacious strategy for enhancing the therapeutic availability of genistein.

In the treatment of periodontitis, an acid-responsive genistein polymer conjugated with 1,4,4'-trimethylenedipiperidine and polyethylene glycol acrylate can be designed. Upon incorporating genistein into its hydrophobic backbone, this polymer self-assembles into micelles in aqueous conditions due to its amphiphilic nature. Importantly, it rapidly releases genistein under acidic conditions. This design addresses the issue of genistein's poor water solubility and possesses a pathological stimulation response ability for controlled release, thereby offering a promising new strategy for the treatment of periodontitis.
Hydrogel

Hydrogel is a semi-solid gel with water as the dispersion medium. It is usually a hydrophilic three-dimensional network structure. It is a crosslinked polymer network that is swollen by water, and the content is usually higher than 90% (Wu et al. ). Hydrogel exhibits a wide range of potential applications within the medical field, including but not limited to tissue engineering, wound healing, controlled drug delivery systems, and as biodegradable scaffolds for cell culture and implantation. Encapsulating genistein within hydrogels can optimize its therapeutic effect by safeguarding it from degradation and facilitating its controlled release in vivo. This encapsulation technique enhances the stability and bioavailability of genistein, thereby maximizing its therapeutic potential.

Yang et al.  used genistein encapsulated in hydrogels to alleviate the symptoms of vaginal atrophy and confirmed that the combination of genistein and hydrogels can achieve sustained release of genistein. It has the advantages of strong mucosal affinity and prolonged local retention time and is suitable for transdermal and mucosal administration. In a study, a local hydrogel containing genistein-loaded nanoemulsion was obtained by spontaneous emulsification. Nanoemulsion-based hydrogels incorporating genistein could be regarded as a promising delivery system for isoflavones to the skin (de Vargas et al. ). In addition, Zagorska-Dziok et al.  synthesized a new poly (chitosan-ester-ether-carbamate) hydrogel, which is noncytotoxic to skin cells (keratinocytes and fibroblasts) and has a relatively highly controlled release curve. It is considered to be an effective dermatological and/or cosmetic tool. In another study, Mahajan et al.  formulated a keratin-genistein-based hydrogel for wound healing and showed anti-inflammatory properties, suggesting its potential as a promising therapeutic agent for managing wound repair.

The development of a controlled release genistein hydrogel offers several advantages in the treatment of periodontitis. The sustained release characteristic of the hydrogel preparation allows for long-term antibacterial activity in vitro. Additionally, its bioadhesive property and injectability enhance the topical delivery of natural plant extracts, particularly those containing genistein, into periodontal pockets. This formulation facilitates the insertion of the hydrogel into the periodontal pocket during experimental procedures, ensuring precise placement. Additionally, the hydrogel's controlled release mechanism allows for sustained drug delivery over an extended period, enhancing the efficacy of genistein. This not only improves the therapeutic outcome but also offers a more comfortable treatment experience for patients, potentially increasing their compliance with the treatment regimen.
Solid Dispersion

Solid dispersion refers to a kind of solid dispersion formed by highly dispersing insoluble drugs in solid dispersion materials by certain methods (Huang and Dai ). Solid dispersion can highly disperse drugs to form molecular, colloidal, microcrystalline, or amorphous dispersion states, which can greatly improve the dissolution and absorption of drugs (Jin et al. ). Solid dispersion technology is a technology that the drug is highly dispersed in another solid carrier material by a certain method to form a solid dispersion. The encapsulation of genistein in solid dispersions can enhance its therapeutic efficacy by improving its dissolution profile and facilitating in vivo absorption.

It has been studied that the genistein-nano-silica solid dispersion was prepared by the solvent method and the conversion of genistein was (93.47 +- 2.40) % (Andhariya and Burgess ). Qiu et al.  prepared solid dispersions of genistein using the solvent rotary evaporation method, with polyvinylpyrrolidone K30 serving as the carrier. The solid dispersion of genistein could represent a promising formulation strategy for enhancing the dissolution rate and improving oral bioavailability. Serebrenik et al.  developed an amorphous solid dispersion of genistein using hot melt extrusion for prophylactic administration to improve the survival rate of samples after radiation exposure.

A new type of drug preparation, solid dispersion, was prepared by highly dispersing genistein in periodontal tissue engineering scaffolds. This formulation enhances the dissolution, sustained release, and targeted delivery of genistein, making it more effective in periodontal tissue regeneration engineering. Additionally, genistein's pharmacological activities, including its anti-inflammatory properties and osteogenic differentiation capabilities, are likely to be more pronounced with this drug preparation. Therefore, this innovative solid dispersion approach has the potential to significantly improve the outcomes of periodontitis treatment and periodontal tissue regeneration.
Microsphere

Microspheres are drug-loaded systems in which drugs are dispersed or adsorbed on carriers, and microspheres of 1-500 mum are formed by microencapsulation technology, and then various dosage forms are made according to the clinical route of administration and therapeutic use (Cai, Chen, et al. ). This special drug dosage form enables the drug to be effectively fixed and dispersed in the micro-skeleton of polymer materials, thus possessing a series of unique properties and application advantages. As a new type of drug dosage form, microspheres show a wide range of application potential in the field of drug carriers. They have a variety of administration routes, including oral, injection, and topical administration, so as to meet the needs of different disease treatments.

In order to address the solubility issues of genistein and facilitate controlled release, studies have been conducted on the microencapsulation of genistein extracted from soybeans using spray-drying techniques to obtain solid dispersions. This method has shown promise in overcoming the solubility limitations of genistein and enhancing its therapeutic potential (Panizzon et al. ). In addition, chitosan microspheres loaded with genistein were successfully fabricated utilizing the double emulsion method. This technique yields microspheres characterized by excellent shape uniformity, high production efficiency, and notable sustained release capabilities (Wu and Li ).

Microsphere-based scaffolds are regarded as suitable materials for bone and cartilage injury repair due to their microporous structure, which offers ample internal space conducive to cell proliferation and other cellular activities. In the context of periodontal disease treatment, microsphere scaffolds have the potential to enhance the bioavailability of genistein. By incorporating genistein into these scaffolds, more effective delivery of the drug to the target site can be ensured, thereby augmenting its therapeutic efficacy. Consequently, microsphere scaffolds present a promising strategy for improving the treatment of periodontal disease through optimized genistein delivery. Figure 4 shows the partial drug delivery system of genistein and its advantages.

Partial drug delivery system of genistein and its advantages. To enhance genistein's bioavailability, various strategies have been employed, with nanoparticles, liposomes, polymer micelles, hydrogels, solid dispersions, and microspheres being the most common.
Discussion

Our research focuses on the investigation of the diverse pharmacological effects of genistein within the pathogenic mechanisms of periodontitis. Through rigorous analysis, it is possible to identify key molecular targets of genistein's action, which may offer novel perspectives for the prevention and treatment of periodontitis. Furthermore, recent studies have demonstrated that various drug delivery systems for genistein enhance its bioavailability, subsequently improving therapeutic outcomes. Consequently, genistein can be regarded as an efficacious therapeutic adjuvant.

The soft-hard tissue interface of the human periodontium plays a critical role in maintaining periodontal homeostasis and is indispensable for normal oral function. This interface is shaped by a complex interplay of physical, chemical, and biological factors. Periodontal ligament stem cells (PDLSCs) are localized at the interface between the soft and hard tissues of the periodontium (Dang et al. ). Additionally, estrogen stimulates PDLSCs and enhances their osteogenic differentiation, with these effects demonstrating a concentration-dependent relationship (Cai, Yuan, et al. ). Notably, genistein may modulate estrogen-mediated processes in the treatment of periodontitis, thereby contributing to the regulation of homeostasis at the interface between the soft and hard tissues of the human periodontium.

Dental calculus comprises inorganic components and an organic matrix derived from saliva, gingival crevicular fluid, and bacterial byproducts (Wei et al. ). Dental calculus serves as a local contributing factor in the pathogenesis of periodontitis (D'souza et al. ). The primary goal of periodontitis treatment is to eliminate inflammation, halt the progression of the disease, and ultimately facilitate the regeneration of tooth-supporting tissues. Conventional basic scaling is effective in removing only a portion of dental calculus and plaque, indicating certain limitations in its efficacy. Genistein, a natural compound with diverse biological activities, is employed as an adjuvant therapeutic agent in the management of periodontitis. The pharmacological properties and mechanisms of genistein in the treatment of periodontal disease are primarily centered on two key aspects: inhibiting periodontal soft tissue destruction and inhibiting alveolar bone destruction.

Genistein not only inhibits periodontal soft tissue destruction but also has been shown to protect alveolar bone by inhibiting osteoclasts and promoting osteogenesis. It down-regulates the expression of inflammatory mediators by regulating various signaling pathways such as NF-kappaB, MAPK, and iNOS/NO and inhibits the damage of inflammation to periodontal tissue. In terms of protecting alveolar bone, genistein can replace estrogen to effectively prevent the reduction of alveolar bone height caused by estrogen deficiency in early menopause and reduce the risk of tooth loss. Genistein can not only act on the OPG/RANK/RANKL signal axis, reduce the RANKL/OPG ratio, and inhibit the activity of osteoclasts but it can also effectively reduce the bone loss of ovariectomized rats. It can also activate the MAPK signaling pathway in mouse bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells in a dose-dependent manner, promote new bone formation, and play a role in bone protection.

The disruption of the balance between osteoblasts and osteoclasts by inflammatory cytokines constitutes the primary cause of bone loss (Usui et al. ). In the periodontal inflammatory microenvironment, bacterial lipopolysaccharide interacts with monocytes to produce a variety of cytokines. These cytokines (such as TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-1beta, and IL-17) play a role in the bone destruction pathway of periodontitis and can cause bone resorption by regulating osteoclast formation (Ramadan et al. ). In addition to inducing the inflammatory response, TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-1beta, and IL-17 can regulate osteoclast differentiation. TNF-alpha can induce osteoclast differentiation of macrophages by directly increasing the expression of RANK in macrophages or enhancing RANKL signal transduction (Kitaura et al. ). IL-6 not only promotes the differentiation of bone marrow-derived macrophages into osteoclasts but also synergizes with IL-1 to accelerate bone loss in ovariectomized rats (Dai et al. ). Moreover, the combination of TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IL-1beta significantly increased the ratio of RANKL/OPG in cells and enhanced osteoclast activity (Blaschke et al. ). The exact mechanism by which genistein inhibits ligation-induced alveolar bone destruction is unclear. Various pro-inflammatory mediators, such as NO and IL-6, are present at a high level in the lesion site of periodontal disease and are associated with a higher severity of periodontal disease. In addition, both NO and IL-6 possess the ability to activate osteoclasts and induce bone destruction (Matejka et al. ; Pelt et al. ). Therefore, regulating the excessive production of these destructive mediators seems to have a protective effect on alveolar bone destruction caused by periodontal disease.

The low water solubility of genistein limits its application in periodontitis. All kinds of new genistein drug delivery systems show excellent solubility, targeting, and sustained release properties, which can overcome the problems of poor water solubility of drugs. It can accurately deliver drugs to the lesion site, continuously and stably release drugs, and effectively prolong the action time of drugs. Given that genistein exhibits excellent pharmacological activities such as anti-inflammatory and osteogenic promotion, its high melting point and low water solubility greatly limit its application potential in the treatment of periodontal disease. In order to solve this problem, we can explore the optimization of the drug delivery system of genistein in order to overcome its inherent physical obstacles and improve its solubility in saliva, which provides more choices for the product design of genistein in the field of periodontitis.

In a number of basic studies, genistein is usually administered immediately after animal periodontitis model establishment. However, in the clinical environment, genistein may be used in the development or middle and late stages of periodontal disease. Consequently, further research is warranted to thoroughly evaluate the potential of genistein as a therapeutic agent for patients suffering from periodontitis. Although genistein has shown multi-dimensional therapeutic potential in periodontitis-related research, there are few studies on its application in the treatment of periodontitis patients in clinical trials, and its development potential, related mechanism, and safety remain to be further studied.
Overall Conclusions and Future Perspectives

Genistein, a versatile phytoestrogen, exhibits a wide array of biological activities in mammals, functioning as both an estrogen agonist and antagonist. However, its health-promoting attributes transcend its estrogenic mimicry. Preclinical studies have documented numerous pharmacological activities of genistein, encompassing anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antibacterial, anti-osteoporotic, anti-tumor, and estrogen-like effects. In the context of periodontitis, genistein demonstrates a potent ability to suppress the mRNA and protein expression of inflammatory mediators, including IL-1beta, TNF-alpha, COX-2, IL-6, IL-17a, ICAM-1, and PGE2, thereby exhibiting significant anti-inflammatory activity in the periodontal inflammatory response. Furthermore, genistein modulates bone metabolism by inhibiting the expression of RANKL and augmenting the expression of OPG, while simultaneously enhancing the expression of AKP and BGP. These actions collectively contribute to bone protection and mitigate the progression of periodontal tissue destruction. Emerging evidence from existing research robustly supports the therapeutic efficacy of genistein in the prevention and treatment of periodontal disease, highlighting its diverse pharmacological activities in periodontal tissue. However, the current body of research examining the effects of genistein on periodontal disease remains limited, and the underlying mechanisms of its potential therapeutic action have yet to be fully elucidated. Further research is needed to provide a more scientific basis for clinical periodontal treatment.

Genistein possesses antibacterial properties; however, to date, there have been no reports on the relationship between genistein and the major pathogenic bacteria associated with periodontitis. The antibacterial capabilities of genistein present a promising avenue for further research into its potential applications in the treatment of periodontitis-related pathogens. By examining the interaction between genistein and pathogenic bacteria associated with periodontitis, new insights may be gained into the mechanisms by which genistein inhibits bacterial growth and virulence, ultimately paving the way for the development of innovative therapeutic strategies for this condition.

The limited aqueous solubility of genistein hampers its application in the treatment of periodontitis, prompting a surge in research aimed at enhancing its bioavailability. A variety of novel drug delivery systems for genistein have been developed to tackle the challenge of its poor solubility. Local administration of these systems not only mitigates systemic side effects but also ensures targeted delivery of the drug to the site of the lesion, thereby maximizing its therapeutic efficacy. Moving forward, the conduct of additional clinical trials and studies utilizing genistein preparations with superior bioavailability holds the promise of unlocking new frontiers in the field of periodontal research.

passages.text: Leveraging diverse cell-death patterns to predict to predict prognosis and immunotherapy in hepatocellular carcinoma
Background

Currently, liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) is characterized by high morbidity, rapid progression and early metastasis. Although many efforts have been made to improve the prognosis of LIHC, the situation is still dismal. Inability to initiate the process of programmed cell death (PCD) is closely associated with cancer progression, thus influencing patients' prognosis. In this study, our purpose was to construct PCD-related prognostic signature for LIHC patients.
Methods

The list of PCD-related genes was obtained from GSEA gene sets. The gene set associated with survival time and survival status was screened by weighted correlation network analysis (WGCNA). Via Cox regression test and LASSO Cox regression model, prognostic signature was established and was then externally validated by ICGC-LIRI-JP dataset and GSE14520 dataset. The immune infiltration status and immune function of the signature were analyzed by ESTIMATE algorithm and ssGSEA algorithm. TIDE score, IPS and immune checkpoints expression and IC50 value were utilized to predict chemosensitivity and immunotherapy response. Moreover, GSE91061 dataset and PRJEB23709 dataset were enrolled to verify the predictive efficacy on immunotherapy response.
Results

A total of 89 genes correlated with survival time and survival status were screened out from 1249 PCD-related genes. Next, the prognostic signature consisting of GLA, CLTA, CHGA, ERP29, MAPK3, CDK5, NLE1, STYXL1 and SFN was constructed. And high-risk patients were related to an adverse prognosis in TCGA-LIHC cohort and ICGC-LIRI-JP cohort. The prognostic signature also showed moderate to high predictive accuracy and was an independent prognostic indicator for LIHC. In general, low-risk patients exhibited higher StromalScore, immune cell infiltration levels, IPS, IPS-PD1 blocker, IPS-CTLA4 blocker, immune checkpoints expression and HLA-related genes expression while lower TIDE score, which indicated low-risk group tended to profit from ICI treatment. Furthermore, responders to ICI treatment had a lower riskscore in GSE91061 cohort, which showed similar result with ours.
Conclusions

Our study developed a novel prognostic signature comprising of 9 PCD-related genes, which could stratify the risk and effectively predict the prognosis and the immunotherapy response of LIHC patients.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s12672-025-03257-w.
Introduction

Liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC), the most common subtype of primary liver cancer, ranks as the second deadliest cancer globally. In recent years, both the incidence and mortality rates of LIHC have shown a gradual upward trend. Scientists predict that by 2025, LIHC will account for over one million cancer-related deaths. Despite well-established risk factors such as HBV infection, aflatoxin B1 exposure, and liver cirrhosis, and the widespread use of comprehensive treatment strategies:including surgery, chemotherapy, targeted drug therapy, immunotherapy, and liver transplantation:the 5-year survival rate remains dismally low at less than 20%, with early diagnosis rates below 30% in some developing countries. Additionally, high treatment costs, severe adverse drug reactions, and limited access to advanced diagnostic and therapeutic technologies further hinder patient participation in treatment. Consequently, the overall survival outcomes for LIHC patients remain unsatisfactory. Moreover, as research into tumor heterogeneity deepens, traditional prognostic assessments based solely on TNM staging are becoming increasingly inadequate. Therefore, developing a prognostic signature grounded in the molecular profiles of LIHC holds significant promise for improving patient outcomes.

Cancers are strongly associated with the disruption or the aberrant regulation of cell growth and death. After a long time in research and practice, resisting cell death is considered as one of the hallmarks of cancer. The main patterns of cell death contain accidental cell death (ACD) and programmed cell death (PCD). PCD is usually controlled by tightly structured signaling and elaborate mechanisms, while the occurrence and progression of ACD are random and uncontrollable. Currently, known PCD patterns primarily include apoptosis, autophagy, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, entotic cell death, oxeiptosis, alkaliptosis, necroptosis, cuproptosis, netotic cell death, parthanatos, and lysosome-dependent cell death. According to the different molecular mechanisms and function characteristics among PCD patterns, researchers pointedly develop drugs to regulate the process of PCD, thus suppressing tumor growth and eliminating cancer cells. BCL-2 inhibitors, classical apoptosis regulators, were widely utilized in the treatment of hematologic malignancies. Gasdermin released by NP-GSDMA3 could induce inflammation-related pyroptosis, and it could increase sensitivity to anti-PD-L1 treatment. In the treatment of triple negative breast cancer, gefitinib sensitivity increased through inducing GPX4-mediated ferroptosis. Previous studies had reported that some members of PCD-related genes were associated with patients' prognosis in various human tumor types. For example, high expression of DAPK3, a apoptosis-related gene, was related to an unfavorable prognosis in colon cancer. And elevated expression of GPX4, the key gene of ferroptosis, was associated with longer disease-free survival (DFS) in patients with breast cancer treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy. FDX1 was identified as the vital gene in the process of cuproptosis and high expression group showed a favorable prognosis in clear cell renal cell carcinoma. Thus, exploring the significance of PCD-related genes in prognostic evaluation and tailored therapy as well as their correlations with immune microenvironment is of great value.

Although some previous publications have established gene signatures according to specific pattern of PCD, comprehensive summary of the relationship between PCD-related genes and LIHC via in silico methods is lacking. In the present study, we collected and analyzed the expression status, mutation status and prognostic performance of PCD-related genes in LIHC. And we built up and verified a PCD-related prognostic signature using integrated expression data and survival data. Besides, the correlations between tumor immune microenvironment, immune checkpoint blockade response, chemotherapy sensitivity and the signature were also evaluated. The current study may offer powerful evidences on risk stratification, prognosis evaluation, chemotherapy drug selection and immunotherapy of LIHC.
Materials and methods
Data collection and preparation

In the present study, gene expression profiling data and corresponding clinical characteristics of LIHC patients were extracted from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database (https://portal.gdccancer.gov/repository), Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/) and International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC) database (https://dcc.icgc.org/), respectively. More specifically, TCGA-LIHC dataset, containing 370 patients, was utilized as the training group to construct the machine learning model. Next, the prognostic power of the above model was validated by GSE14520 dataset (n = 242) from GEO database and ICGC-LIRI-JP dataset (n = 260). The patients with survival data missing would be excluded. In addition, the two immunotherapy cohorts from GEO database, GSE91061 (n = 98) and PRJEB23709 (n = 94), were enrolled to validate predictive power of immunotherapy response of the model.

We also collected the primary regulatory genes of 12 diverse PCD patterns, including apoptosis, autophagy, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, entotic cell death, oxeiptosis, alkaliptosis, necroptosis, cuproptosis, netotic cell death, parthanatos, and lysosome-dependent cell death, from GSEA gene sets (http://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/), KEGG, Genecards, and recent reviews on January 9, 2023. After manually collating the gene list, 1249 PCD-related genes were eventually included in the subsequent analyses (Supplementary Table 1).
Weighted correlation network analysis and module selection

Weighted correlation network analysis (WGCNA) is a biostatistics method used to describe patterns of gene associations between different samples. Rather than focusing only on differentially expressed genes, WGCNA can utilize information from thousands of the most varied genes or all genes to identify gene sets of interest and conduct correlation analysis with phenotypes. In this study, we built up a scale-free coexpression network in TCGA-LIHC dataset based on "WGCNA" package in R software. The soft-threshold value (beta value) was selected under the degree of independence of 0.9. The minimal module size was set as 30. Based on Pearson correlation analysis, a matrix was generated to assess the module-trait relationships between PCD-related genes and survival status, and survival time. The modules with P-value of less than 0.05 were identified as the key modules and were selected to conduct further analyses.
Non-negative matrix factorization clustering analysis

According to the expression profile of selected genes from WGCNA, non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) algorithm was used to distinguish various PCD-related patterns. NMF clustering split the original matrix into multiple non-negative matrices, and it redeposited and aggregated the results to generate stable clustering, thus selecting out potential features. The optimal clustering number (K value) was identified based on corresponding cophenetic, dispersion, and silhouette index. And the processes of NMF clustering was performed using "NMF" package.
Survival analysis, prognostic model construction and nomogram establishment

The PCD-related genes selected by WGCNA were firstly assessed by univariate Cox regression test before building up prognostic model. The P-value threshold was set as 0.001 in this process. Via "glmnet" package in R, these potential prognostic PCD-related genes were next included in the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression test to confirm the number of genes in the final prognostic model. The selected genes in LASSO regression test were performed multivariate Cox regression test, sequentially establishing the prognostic model and generating the formula of risk score as follow: . Expi was the expression value of each selected gene, and the Coei was the corresponding multivariable Cox regression coefficient. Selecting the median risk score as cutoff, patients were assigned to high-risk and low-risk group. Overall survival curves of the two groups were compared by Kaplan-Meier analysis in "survival" package. Time ROC curve, clinical ROC curve and decision curve were used to evaluate predictive accuracy of the prognostic model through "timeROC" package and "DecisionCurve" package. Moreover, to compare the performance of our model with others, we also reconstructed the prognostic model in some previous publications and calculate their C-indices by "CompareC" package.

For better predicting the prognosis of LIHC patients, a nomogram integrating the prognostic model and clinical characteristics, containing age, gender and clinical stage, was also established by "rms" package. And the corresponding calibration curve was constructed to compare the fitting degree between the ideal and the actual survival probabilities.
Mutation landscape and tumor immune microenvironment evaluation

We next visualized the somatic mutation status as waterfall plot by "maftools" package and assessed the tumor mutation burden (TMB) between high- and low-risk group. Standardized somatic mutation data of the samples in TCGA-LIHC dataset was acquired from UCSC Xena (https://xena.ucsc.edu/). The Immune score, ESTIMATE score and Stromal score in high- and low-risk group were calculated through estimation of stromal and immune cells in malignant tumor tissues using expression data (ESTIMATE) algorithm. Based on single sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) algorithm, immune infiltration level of 16 kinds of immune cells in high- and low-risk group were calculated by "GSVA" package. Related immune cell activity and function were also quantified via "GSVA" package. The expression levels of common immune checkpoints and human leukocyte antigen (HLA) -related genes between high- and low-risk group were also compared through "ggpubr" package.
Gene set enrichment analysis

To explore differences of biological functions and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway between high- and low-risk group, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was conducted via "GSVA" and "GSEABase" package. The threshold of GSEA was set as FDR < 0.05 and q-value < 0.2.
Immunotherapeutic response analysis and chemotherapy drug sensitivity analysis

The tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion (TIDE) score was downloaded from the TIDE platform (http://tide.dfci.harvard.edu) and was compared between high- and low-risk group. Immunophenoscore (IPS), a predictor of response to ICI therapy, was also downloaded from The Cancer Immunome Atlas (TCIA) (https://tcia.at/home) and was compared between high- and low-risk patients. In addition, we externally validated the risk model on immunotherapeutic response. Owing to the lack of publicly available dataset concerning immune-checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) treatment focusing on LIHC patients, GSE91061 dataset (Anti-PD1 treatment) and PRJEB23709 dataset (Anti-PD1 or Anti-CTLA4 treatment) comprising patients with advanced melanoma were selected. Patients with complete response (CR)/partial response (PR) to immunotherapy were identified as responders, while patients with stable disease (SD)/progressive disease (PD) were identified as non-responders.

Data of drug sensitivity was downloaded from Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) (https://www.cancerrxgene.org/). Using "oncoPredict" package, half maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) value of chemotherapy and targeted drugs was compared between high- and low-risk group. A lower IC50 value was correlated with a higher drug sensitivity.
Statistical analyses

All visualization and statistical analyses in the current study were conducted in R software Version 4.1.2. Comparisons between two groups were evaluated by Student's t-test or Wilcoxon test. Kruskal-Wallis test was conducted in multi-group comparison. A two-sided P-value cutoff was set as 0.05. In addition, the flowchart concerning the study design was shown in Fig. 1.

Results
Weighted gene co-expression network construction and key module selection

Through preprocessing the expression profiles of 370 patients in TCGA-LIHC dataset, the expression matrices of the 1249 PCD-related genes were generated. Gene names of the 1249 genes and corresponding PCD subtypes were provided in Supplementary Table 1. Using the above data, weighted gene co-expression network was constructed to determine key modules associated with survival status and survival time of LIHC patients. As shown in Fig. 2A, the soft threshold power of 6 was the most efficient to perform a scale-free network with the degree of independence of 0.9. Clustering tree was classified the genes into 4 differentially colored modules (Fig. 2B). Next, the association between each module and survival status, and survival time was analyzed by Pearson's correlation test. Comprehensively considered the correlation coefficient among these 4 modules, the brown module, including 89 genes, was identified as the key module associated with overall survival time (cor=-0.16, P-value = 0.002) and overall survival status (cor = 0.16, P-value = 0.002) (Fig. 2C). The gene list was shown in Supplementary Table 2.

Molecular subgroup clustering analysis

The expression profiles of the 89 genes selected by WGCNA were next classified into different molecular subtypes based on NMF clustering algorithm, patients with similar molecular subtypes were assigned to corresponding cluster. According to the cophenetic, dispersion, and silhouette index in TCGA-LIHC dataset, the cluster number K of 3 was the optimal. The heatmap of corresponding consensus matrices were also visualized in Fig. 3A. The cluster result was verified in GSE14520 dataset (Fig. 3B) and ICGC-LIRI-JP dataset (Fig. 3C). In the survival analysis of TCGA-LIHC dataset (Fig. 3D, P-value = 0.038), GSE14520 dataset (Fig. 3E, P-value < 0.001) and ICGC-LIRI-JP dataset (Fig. 3F, P-value = 0.003), there were statistical differences among C1, C2 and C3. However, more in-depth studies are urgently needed to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms.

Survival analysis and prognostic signature construction

Using genomic data from TCGA-LIHC cohort, the prognostic performance of the 89 genes from WGCNA were analyzed via univariate Cox regression test. As a result, a total of 13 PCD-related genes were selected out and were defined as the prognostic-related genes. More specifically, high expression of AATF, ERP29, HRAS, NLE1, SFN, STYXL1, OTUB1, CDK5, MAPK3, AP4M1, CHGA, CLTA and GLA was related to a worse prognosis in LIHC patients (Fig. 4, all P-value < 0.001). Next, LASSO Cox regression method was utilized to analyze these 13 prognostic-related genes, and finally identified 9 genes (ERP29, NLE1, SFN, STYXL1, CDK5, MAPK3, CHGA, CLTA and GLA) for prognostic risk model construction. In Fig. 5A and B, partial likelihood deviance and coefficients of the prognostic risk model were shown. Riskscore = (0.07448)*ERP29 expression + (0.05618)*NLE1 expression + (0.06079)*SFN expression + (0.09877)*STYXL1 expression + (0.10224)*CDK5 expression + (0.01606)*MAPK3 expression + (0.14257)*CHGA expression + (0.20325)*CLTA expression + (0.09510)*GLA expression. Patients were divided into high- and low-risk group based on median risk score. In TCGA-LIHC dataset, high-risk group showed a worse prognosis compared to low-risk group (P-value < 0.001, Fig. 5C). Next, GSE14520 dataset and ICGC-LIRI-JP dataset were utilized to validate predictive performance of the prognostic signature, and similar survival outcomes also existed in ICGC-LIRI-JP dataset (P-value < 0.001, Fig. 5E). However, in GSE14520 dataset, marginal statistical difference was detected between high- and low-risk group (P-value = 0.072, Fig. 5D). Moreover, the risk score distribution, survival status and expression status of each sample in TCGA-LIHC dataset, GSE14520 dataset and ICGC-LIRI-JP dataset were illustrated in Fig. 5F, G and H, respectively. The clinical ROC curves of corresponding cohorts were established. In TCGA-LIHC dataset, AUC values of age, gender, clinical stage and riskscore were 0.537, 0.513, 0.664 and 0.756, respectively (Fig. 6A). In GSE14520 dataset, AUC values of age, gender, clinical stage and riskscore were 0.570, 0.535, 0.689 and 0.604, respectively (Fig. 6B). In ICGC-LIRI-JP dataset, AUC values of age, gender, clinical stage and riskscore were 0.463, 0.419, 0.815 and 0.733, respectively (Fig. 6C). Time ROC analysis was also performed in these 3 cohorts. The 1-year, 3-year and 5-year AUC values of TCGA-LIHC dataset were 0.756, 0.681 and 0.667 (Fig. 6D). The 1-year, 3-year and 5-year AUC values of GSE14520 dataset were 0.604, 0.591 and 0.579 (Fig. 6E). The 1-year, 3-year and 5-year AUC values of ICGC-LIRI-JP dataset were 0.733, 0.746 and 0.710 (Fig. 6F). Furthermore, C-indices of riskscore were highest in most of the time (Fig. 6G-I). Comprehensively considering the results of clinical ROC analysis and time ROC analysis, and C-indices of clinical features and riskscore, our model had a good predictive performance. To explore the potential factors that affected LIHC patients' prognosis, univariate and multivariate Cox regression analysis were conducted in TCGA-LIHC dataset (Fig. 7A and B), GSE14520 dataset (Fig. 7C and D) and ICGC-LIRI-JP dataset (Fig. 7E and F), which identified risk score and clinical stage as independent risk factors.

Signature comparison and nomogram establishment

To compare our model with other program cell death signature, including anoikis-related signature, pyroptosis-related signature, necroptosis-related signature, lysosome-related signature, ferroptosis-related signature, autophagy-related signature, cuproptosis-related signature, and apoptosis-related signature; we collected expression profiles and survival data from previous publications. Using collected data from TCGA-LIHC dataset, we utilized the same statistical methods to calculate the risk score and to establish the risk model based on the genes described in corresponding publications. All P-value of the survival curves were less than 0.05. And C-index of each signature was also calculated and compared, and our model had the highest C-index of 0.688, indicating an advanced performance (Fig. 8).
Comparison with other signatures. C-index comparison among the 9 signatures

To offer a quantitative method for prognostic evaluation of LIHC patients based on our signature, a nomogram that integrated the risk model and clinical parameters, containing gender, age and clinical stage, was generated using the data from TCGA-LIHC dataset. Each item was assigned to the corresponding score, and a higher total score revealed a lower 1-year, 3-year and 5-year survival rate (Fig. 9A). The 1-year, 3-year and 5-year calibration plots were compared with the ideal model and showed a good fitting between actual value and optimized value (Fig. 9B). The clinical ROC curve revealed the nomogram had a good predictive efficacy with the highest AUC value of 0.728 (Fig. 9C). Moreover, the DCA result also illustrated the high potential of the nomogram in clinical application (Fig. 9D).

Mutation status and immune microenvironment between high- and low-risk group

Using mutation data from TCGA-LIHC dataset, the overall somatic mutation status in high- and low-risk group was also analyzed. The top 15 most frequently mutated genes in high- and low-risk group were visualized in Supplementary Fig. 1A-B. As shown in Fig. 10C, low-risk group had a higher TMB level than high-risk group (Supplementary Fig. 1C, P-value < 0.01). There was no significant difference of ESTIMATEScore (P-value = 0.33, Supplementary Fig. 1D) and ImmuneScore (P-value = 0.26, Supplementary Fig. E) between high- and low-risk group, while a significant higher StromalScore (P-value = 0.00039, Supplementary Fig. 1F) existed in low-risk group. The infiltration levels of the 16 immune cell subtypes in the two groups were compared by ssGSEA algorithm. Low-risk patients had a higher infiltrating level of B cells, CD8 + T cells, mast cells, neutrophils, NK cells, T helper cells, Th2 cells and TIL cells, while high-risk patients had a higher infiltration level of macrophages (Supplementary Fig. 1G, all P-value < 0.05). The ssGSEA score of immune functions in the two groups was also assessed. Compared to those with high-risk, patients in low-risk group showed higher scores in CCR level, cytolytic activity, T cell co-stimulation and type-II IFN response and lower scores in MHC class I level (all P-value < 0.05, Supplementary Fig. H). MHC class I molecules play a crucial role in adaptive immune responses. Acting as sentinels of the immune system, they present antigen peptides in a unique way on the cell surface, thereby activating CD8 + T cells. However, tumor cells can also evolve under T cell selection to impair the antigen-presenting ability of MHC class I molecules. Thus, HCC patients with high risk score may have high level of MHC class I molecules but low level of CD8 + T cell.

Gene set enrichment analysis

GSEA was performed to explore potential molecular mechanisms and pathways of our prognostic signature. Top 5 enriched KEGG items in high- and low-risk group were showed in Supplementary Fig. 2A-B, respectively. High-risk group was mainly associated with cell cycle, cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, ECM receptor interaction, hematopoietic cell lineage and ribosome, while low-risk group was mainly correlated to complement and coagulation cascades, fatty acid metabolism, glycine serine and threonine metabolism, primary bile acid biosynthesis and retinol metabolism.
Immunotherapy response prediction between high- and low-risk group

The difference of TIDE score between the two groups was assessed. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 2C, high-risk group had a higher TIDE score than low-risk group (P-value < 0.001). And IPS, IPS-PD1 blocker, IPS-CTLA4 blocker and IPS-CTLA4 + PD1 blocker in high- and low-risk group were compared. Compared to high-risk patients, IPS (P-value = 0.0039, Supplementary Fig. 2D), IPS-PD1 blocker (P-value = 0.0430, Supplementary Fig. 2E) and IPS-CTLA4 blocker (P-value = 0.0200, Supplementary Fig. 2 F) were significantly higher in low-risk patients. While, no statistical difference was detected in IPS-CTLA4 + PD1 blocker between the two groups (P-value = 0.1000, Supplementary Fig. 2G). The expression levels of common immune checkpoints between these two groups were also analyzed. Compared with low-risk patients, IDO2 expression was significantly elevated in high-risk group (P-value < 0.05). Nevertheless, the expression levels of other 29 immune checkpoints were significantly decreased in high-risk group (all P-value < 0.05, Supplementary Fig. 2H). As for HLA-related markers, the expression levels of all 24 markers were significantly decreased in high-risk group (all P-value < 0.05, Supplementary Fig. 2I). These results suggested that patients in low-risk group might be more likely to benefit from ICI treatment.
External validation of immunotherapy response between high- and low-risk group

To verify predictive efficacy of the signature on ICI treatment, the immunotherapy cohorts, including GSE91061 cohort and PRJEB23709 cohort, were enrolled. Based on treatment outcomes, patients were divided into responders (CR/PR group) and non-responders (SD/PD group). Risk score of each patient in these two cohorts was calculated using the same method, and patients were divided into high- and low-risk group according to the median riskscore. In GSE91061 cohort, responders had a lower riskscore than non-responders (P-value = 0.0200, Fig. 10A). Survival analysis revealed patients with high riskscore were related to a worse prognosis (P-value = 0.0500, Fig. 10B). The 1-year and 3-year AUC values were 0.551 and 0.607, respectively (Fig. 10C). These results were similar with the results of our signature. In PRJEB23709 cohort, no statistical difference in riskscore was detected between responders and non-responders (P-value = 0.2100, Fig. 10D). And no difference was also detected in survival analysis between the two groups (P-value = 0.5600, Fig. 10E). The 1-year and 3-year AUC values were 0.536 and 0.560, respectively (Fig. 10F).
Drug sensitivity analysis between high- and low-risk group

Based on drug sensitivity data from GDSC, the correlation between riskscore and IC50 value of some targeted or chemotherapy drugs used against LIHC was analyzed. Low-risk patients were more sensitive to sorafenib (P-value < 2.22e-16, Supplementary Fig. 3 A), vorinostat (P-value = 0.0011, Supplementary Fig. 3B), ruxolitinib (P-value = 7.4e-05, Supplementary Fig. 3 C), oxaliplatin (P-value = 6.7e-09, Supplementary Fig. 3D), axitinib (P-value = 5.3e-13, Supplementary Fig. 3E), cytarabine (P-value = 2.8e-14, Supplementary Fig. 3 F), gemcitabine (P-value = 1.2e-09, Supplementary Fig. 3G), ribociclib (P-value = 3.1e-06, Supplementary Fig. 3H), epirubicin (P-value = 0.0012, Supplementary Fig. 3I), leflunomide (P-value = 6.6e-11, Supplementary Fig. 3 J), mitoxantrone (P-value = 1.9e-12, Supplementary Fig. 3 K) and topotecan (P-value = 5.3e-16, Supplementary Fig. 3L). These results indicated that low-risk patients might be more likely to benefit from targeted therapy and chemotherapy.
Discussion

LIHC is the malignant tumor with high rates of recurrence and metastasis, which causes a disproportionate health burden to patients. The overall 5-year survival rate of LIHC patients was less than 20%. Due to insidious onset, early asymptomatic manifestations, and rapid development, more than 70% of LIHC patients progressed to middle or terminal stages before definitive diagnosis. Ample evidences suggested that avoiding PCD was a one of the common signs in malignances, containing LIHC. PCD includes various and complicated subroutines, which co-regulate cancer progression and the treatment response. With the development of sequencing technique and establishment of genome databases, large-scale and comprehensive analyses on PCD-related genes in LIHC become feasible. However, comprehensive bioinformatic analyses focusing on the prognostic performance of PCD-related genes in LIHC as well as their associations with immune microenvironment and individualized treatment is lacking.

Herein, a gene signature including 9 PCD-related genes, ERP29, NLE1, SFN, STYXL1, CDK5, MAPK3, CHGA, CLTA and GLA, was constructed, which revealed that high-risk group was related to a worse prognosis in TCGA-LIHC dataset and ICGC-LIRI-JP dataset. And riskscore was identified as an independent risk factor using univariate and multivariate Cox regression analysis. And time ROC analysis and clinical ROC analysis revealed the prediction model generally showed moderate to high predictive accuracy. Compared with other 8 gene signatures published in previous studies, our signature had the highest C-index of 0.688. As for these 9 genes, LIHC patients with high expression of STYXL1 were associated with an unfavorable prognosis, and STYXL1 could promote LIHC proliferation and inhibit apoptosis of LIHC cells. High CDK5 expression was correlated with poor prognosis in LIHC patients, and knockdown of CDK5 and functional ablation of CDK5 inhibited the growth and metastasis of LIHC cells. Compared with normal liver tissues, the expression level of SFN in LIHC tissues was significantly higher. And knockdown of SFN significantly reduced HCC cell proliferation. In addition, SFN could accelerate cancer cell progression by inducing autophagy. In cancer cells, GLA overexpression accelerated mitochondrial death and apoptosis. The expression and activation of MAPK3 were elevated in human LIHC cells, phosphorylated MAPK3 regulated tumor sensitivity to erastin, which was a common ferroptosis inducer. Serum CHGA level of LIHC patients was significantly higher, and patients with high CHGA level had poor survival rate. Ren et al. reported that knockdown of NLE1 induced apoptosis and inhibited migration of cancer cells. Knockdown of CLTA inhibited efficient tumor cell spreading and migration. In addition, ERP 29 was also considered as a prognostic indicator in osteosarcoma and invasive breast cancer and participated in the process of cancer cell growth and epithelial-mesenchymal transition.

The tumor microenvironment (TME) in liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) is typically characterized by immunosuppressive features, allowing cancer cells to evade immune detection and promote tumor progression and metastasis. For instance, cancer cells can circumvent immune surveillance by impairing the function of dendritic cells (DCs). Moreover, FOXP3 + regulatory T cells (Tregs) suppress the activation and proliferation of anti-tumor effector cells, contributing to an immunosuppressive TME. In our study, we observed that the high-risk group exhibited elevated infiltration of macrophages, while there was a reduction in the infiltration levels of B cells, CD8 + T cells, mast cells, neutrophils, natural killer (NK) cells, T helper cells, Th2 cells, and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs). Additionally, the high-risk group showed a lower StromalScore. These findings indicate distinct differences in the TME between the two risk groups. Currently, immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy is considered a promising approach for treating unresectable cancers and serves as one of the adjuvant therapies following surgery. Our analysis revealed that the expression levels of HLA-related genes and most common immune checkpoints were significantly higher in the low-risk group, suggesting potential variations in immune response and therapeutic sensitivity between the groups. And IPS, IPS-PD1 blocker and IPS-CTLA4 blocker were higher in low-risk group, while TIDE score in high-risk group was significantly higher. According to the theory of "hot" tumor and "cold" tumor, low-risk group might be the "hot" tumor and tended to profit from ICI treatment. Moreover, responders also had a lower riskscore than non-responders in GSE91061 cohort, which showed similar riskscore distribution with ours.

After SHARP trial in 2007 and Asia-Pacific trial in 2008, sorafenib becomes first-line targeted agent for LIHC patients, ushering in the era of targeted treatment. Tailored therapy based on targeted agents and chemotherapy drugs has flourished over the past decade and will be the future of HCC care. In the present study, we compared IC50 value of each commonly used drug in high- and low-risk group and detected that low-risk patients were more sensitive to sorafenib, vorinostat, ruxolitinib, oxaliplatin, axitinib, cytarabine, gemcitabine, ribociclib, epirubicin, leflunomide, mitoxantrone and topotecan, which illustrated that patients with low riskscore might be more suitable for targeted therapy and chemotherapy. However, further studies are needed to expound the underlying mechanisms concerning the difference of drug sensitivity between the two groups.
Limitations

Several limitations should be acknowledged. Firstly, the majority of the analyses were conducted at the mRNA level, and some findings may not be directly applicable to protein-level studies. Secondly, further experimental research is needed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms by which the PCD-related signature influences prognosis, immune cell infiltration, and responses to immunotherapy and chemotherapy. Thirdly, the validation cohort of ICI response were from patients with advanced melanoma owing to the lack of ICI treatment cohort of LIHC patients. We deeply hope subsequent researchers can offer related data for LIHC research. It would be better to explore the role of key gene in the final nine genes by supplementing functional experimental evidence. Moreover, Brown module showed a week correlation with overall survival time and overall survival status. WGCNA is based on the scale-free network model, in which a few nodes (genes) have a high degree of connectivity (influence), while the majority of nodes have a relatively low degree of connectivity. This structure leads to the situation where even if two genes are highly correlated, the difference in their influence within the network may cause their correlation to appear relatively low in the overall network.
Conclusion

In summary, our study developed a PCD-related gene signature for LIHC patients, which aids in predicting prognosis and provides insights into immune cell infiltration, immunotherapy response, and chemotherapy response in these patients. These findings offer novel perspectives for prognostic evaluation and personalized treatment strategies for individuals with LIHC.
