passages.text: Generalized linear modeling of flow cytometry data to analyze immune responses in tuberculosis vaccine research

Tuberculosis (TB) caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) kills ~1.3 million people annually. Accordingly, vaccines and sophisticated analytical tools are necessary to evaluate their effectiveness. To address these challenges, we created a Generalized Linear Model (GLM) framework to evaluate high-dimensional flow cytometry data and the multivariable influences on immune responses, accommodating proportional and non-normal data, and violations of assumptions set by classical statistical evaluations. In naive mice vaccinated with BCG boosted with ID93-GLA-SE, we used GLMs to assess the impact of sex, vaccination, and days post-infection on probabilities of immune cell phenotypes following Mtb challenge. We demonstrate enhanced T cell responses in the lung following BCG + ID93-GLA-SE compared to BCG or ID93-GLA-SE alone, with notable sex differences in humoral immunity. This framework highlights GLMs in assessing complex datasets while enhancing our comprehension of independent continuous and categorical variables on vaccine efficacy, and serves as a foundation for deeper, more complex scenarios.
Introduction

Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is the causative agent of pulmonary Tuberculosis (TB) disease, which is estimated to infect one-quarter of the global population. As the second leading cause of death from a single infectious agent in 2022 after COVID-19, TB claimed ~1.3 million lives and has caused over 1 million deaths per year since 2013. Additionally, an estimated 10.6 million people developed TB in 2022:a 2.8% and 5.7% increase from 2021 and 2020 approximations, respectively. In 2018, The World Health Organization (WHO) established global targets focused on TB treatment, preventative measures, and funding, including a 75% reduction of TB-caused deaths and a 50% reduction in TB-incidence rate by 2025. However, these were not achieved at least partially due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

For more than 100 years, the only licensed vaccine for TB has been Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG), a live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis that best protects neonates and children from meningeal, pulmonary, and disseminated TB. However, the enduring efficacy of the BCG vaccine beyond ~10 years post-vaccination, particularly in adults, remains puzzling and is a subject of debate. This stems from several factors, including the variability in BCG strains utilized, differences in vaccinated populations and geographical regions, and the influence of environmental factors such as pre-exposure conditions.

While BCG shares a 99% genetic similarity with Mtb, the absence of Mtb-specific antigens has led to the development of subunit vaccines capable of eliciting T cell immunity against Mtb. The subunit vaccine ID93-GLA-SE, comprising four Mtb virulence antigens (Rv2608, Rv3619, Rv3620, and Rv1813) along with a synthetic Toll-like receptor 4 agonist, glucopyranosyl lipid adjuvant (GLA), formulated in a stable emulsion (SE), has advanced into human clinical trials as a promising approach in TB prevention. Preclinical studies have demonstrated the tolerability and immunogenicity of ID93-GLA-SE in various animal models, including humans, showing protective effects against Mtb when used as a primary vaccine. Additionally, ID93-GLA-SE has been observed to recruit CD4+ and CD8+ T cells to the lung, enhancing protection against Mtb CFU burden when administered as a booster following BCG vaccination.

Indeed, we have come to understand several mechanisms of action and efficacy of ID93-GLA-SE among other vaccine candidates through immunoprofiling. However, as we investigate deeper into the mechanisms of protection and efficacy of ID93-GLA-SE and other vaccine candidates, it becomes increasingly apparent that grasping the full spectrum of factors influencing vaccine effectiveness is critical for combating TB.

The threat of rising TB cases and persistence of multidrug-resistant TB highlights the importance of vaccine development research and sophisticated analytical tools to improve our understanding of how these vaccines modulate host immunity. A longstanding approach for vaccine evaluation is immunophenotyping via high-dimensional flow cytometry (12 or more colors) which has been a staple in TB research and allows for evaluation of immune profiles, cell activation, and protein expression at the single cell level. This advancement in instrument technology and parameterization ultimately allows for more sophisticated immunophenotyping. The real-world applications of assessing immunity and vaccine effectiveness through flow cytometry are extensive and have evolved alongside the growing complexity of TB intervention strategies and experimental vaccine approaches. The intricacy of experimental variables and diverse immunological profiles among hosts in TB research can result in flow cytometry data variations that push the boundaries of traditional statistical tests, such as Student's t test, Analysis of Variance (ANOVA), and Wilcoxon:as assumptions regarding normality, sample size, equal variances, and equal dispersion may be violated.

In the context of high dimensional flow cytometry, we address the need for a statistical approach applicable across various scenarios and turn to generalized linear modeling (GLM), a versatile and flexible statistical framework that can, either directly or through extensions of the framework, accommodate non-normality, and other violations of the assumptions of classically used tests to evaluate the effect of experimental variables on hypothesized outcomes. GLMs are a tool in TB research evaluating gene expression between active and latent TB infection. However, immunological flow cytometry data is still routinely analyzed using traditional statistical methods. Here, we illustrate our developed GLM framework which can evaluate flow cytometry data and the influence of experimental parameters on immune cell populations in the mouse lung. Our example data spans several time points (days 14, 56, and 90 post-infection) with female and male C57Bl/6 mice as the model organism vaccinated with BCG, ID93-GLA-SE, or BCG + ID93-GLA-SE. In this context, we assess the multivariable impacts of factors such as sex, vaccination status, and days post-infection on the probabilities of select immune phenotypes present in the lungs of Mtb challenged mice.
Results

The GLM framework serves as a versatile alternative to statistical tests traditionally applied in immunology, like ANOVA, with the advantage that it, or extensions of it, can also be applied to a wide range of data distributions, including non-parametric datasets. For example, our example data is proportional and is best modeled by a binomial distribution which captures the two outcomes of success and failure on a finite number of trials. The GLM framework is also effective in handling overdispersion, making it suitable for analyzing diverse data types. We would like to note that ANOVA falls under the umbrella of a GLM and would provide the same result as ANOVA if the assumptions of normality, equal variance, and independent categorical explanatory variables are met. However, an advantage of the GLM framework is that it can also expand beyond ANOVA. Conveniently, GLMs allow for the inclusion of both continuous and categorical explanatory variables to promote a comprehensive analysis of which independent variables:or combinations thereof:influence the dependent variable without being constrained by the traditional assumptions set by ANOVA. Here, we illustrate applying this framework to investigate the probabilities of activated T cells (CD4+ CD44+), cytotoxic T cells (CD8+), and B cells (CD19+) present out of the population of live leukocytes, and discuss how these probabilities are associated with treatment, days since infection, and sex of our animal model and report non-adjusted p values for exploratory analysis. In a supplemental analysis, to further illustrate the framework, we also investigated dendritic cells (CD11b+ CD11c+ ) and natural killer cells (NK1.1+).
Immune population distributions in C57Bl/6 mouse lungs
Distribution and observed proportions of immune populations in vaccinated female and male C57Bl/6 mice infected with Mtb.

Mice were vaccinated with either Saline (control), BCG, ID93-GLA-SE, or BCG+ID93-GLA-SE and infected with Mtb. Lungs were processed for flow cytometry 14-, 56-, and 90-days post infection, and stained for A, B CD4+ CD44+, C, D CD8+, and E, F CD19+. A, C, E Distributions immune cell "success" in mice within each vaccination group. B, D, F Observed proportions of immune populations normalized to live leukocytes.

Following the restructuring of the data into a GLM-compatible format, we initiated our framework through an exploratory lens aimed at understanding the distribution, variability, and observed proportions of immune response "success" within our data set (Fig. 1A-F). To establish trends in the proportional data and document outliers, we simplified our distribution plots by vaccinated group and determined the frequency of "success" of activated T cells, cytotoxic T cells, and B cells out of live leukocytes (Fig. 1A, C, E). With respect to activated T cells and B cells, BCG and BCG + ID93-GLA-SE vaccinated groups displayed wider distributions of "success", whereas the distribution of cytotoxic T cell counts was not clearly associated with vaccination status.

To establish a reference for data quality, which is instrumental in selecting an appropriate model for further analysis, we plotted observed proportions of immune populations normalized to live leukocytes to visualize the distribution and variability of immune responses across vaccinated groups, days post infection and sex (Fig. 1B, D, F). For these proportions as with direct cell count distributions, cytotoxic T cells did not vary by vaccination status. However, we did observe trends among vaccinated groups for activated T cells (Fig. 1B).

In a supplemental analysis aimed at providing further depth to our understanding of the distribution of immune responses with respect to our explanatory variables, we explored patterns for dendritic cells and natural killer cells (Supplementary Fig. 1), and determined patterns related to time were apparent and most likely due to natural innate immune responses rather than vaccination status.

Overall, this preliminary exploratory analysis within the framework provides insights into identifying trends across vaccinated groups. It's important to note that deviations from a normal distribution within each immune population is expected as proportions typically do not follow a normal distribution. Thus, our focus is not on these deviations but rather on the overall trends and patterns observed in the data.
GLM fit and model selection

Our framework involved evaluating which variables best explained the outcome of immune cell phenotypes. To achieve this, we fit two GLMs to the example data for each immune phenotype of interest. Using our analysis of activated T cells as an example, the initial model examined the main effects of variables "group" and "day" while keeping "sex" constant. The subsequent model expanded upon the first by integrating interactions among all three variables.

When fitting a GLM to obtain probabilities, it is best to choose the model which best captures the trends of the observed data to delineate which variables best explain the outcome. Our framework checked for dispersion or deviation from observed values, and we found that the expanded model demonstrated a lower dispersion parameter when fitting in R (1415 compared to 1556). The framework generates an output of each model that displays the estimated coefficients along with their standard errors, t values, and corresponding p values. An example output for activated T cells is shown in (Supplementary Table 1). We followed our GLM fitting with analysis of deviance (drop in deviance) testing to compare the two models. Drop in deviance analysis revealed a significant drop in deviance (p = 0.017) for our expanded model, indicating that our three-way interaction model provided a better fit to the data than the model with only group and day as the explanatory or predictive variables. Furthermore, we calculated the proportion of explained deviance and determined that the expanded model explains a greater proportion of the variability (57%) compared to the simpler model (43%).

From these results, we can infer that the variable "sex" as an interaction term provides the best explanation for model variability and improves model fit in this application of the framework. We conducted similar evaluations for other immune populations, which yielded consistent results favoring the expanded model (details not shown). Therefore, based on drop in deviance testing, an increase in the proportion of explained deviance, and best model fit, we elected to adopt the expanded model for all immune populations as it provides a more comprehensive representation of the underlying relationships between explanatory variables and outcomes.
Multivariable effect on immune cell phenotypes in the mouse lung
Estimated coefficients and odds ratios for immune responses in the infected mouse lung.

A, C, E Estimated coefficients on the outcome of immune responses for CD4+ CD44+, CD8+, and CD19+ cells for each one-, two-, and three-way interactions of group, day and sex derived from GLM logistical model output. B, D, F Odds ratios for exponentiated estimated effects.

The coefficients estimated from our GLM offer insights into the magnitude and direction of the relationship between each explanatory variable and immune cell responses. These coefficients denote the change in the log-odds of the outcome corresponding to a unit change in the predictor variables. In our framework, we computed the estimated effects of each variable and variable combination (i.e., interactions) on the outcome of immune responses (Fig. 2A, C, E). We converted these estimated coefficients into odds ratios to provide an additional measure of the relationships between immune populations and predictor variables and filtered for statistically significant values (p < 0.05) (Fig. 2B, D, F).

Our framework outputs all estimated effects at this stage to aid in identifying associations that, although not meeting the threshold for statistical significance in the current data, may be practically important and warrant further investigation in larger studies. Additionally, the framework provides additional outputs with odds ratios that highlight the associations supported by the data from this experiment, and the likelihood of an event occurring compared to our baseline.

For example, the effectiveness of BCG in enhancing T cell activation is well-documented, and our estimated effects support this (Fig. 2A). However, despite an odds ratio of ~2 based on the estimated log odds ratio, suggesting an increased probability of T cell activation in the female mice vaccinated with BCG on day 14 compared to saline, we did not observe a strong association in odds ratios based on our predetermined significance threshold.

Odds ratios, derived from our model, represent the change in odds of an event occurring for each unit increase in the predictor variables and their interactions. An odds ratio greater than 1 suggests an increased likelihood of the event, while an odds ratio between 0 and 1 suggests a decreased likelihood. An odds ratio of exactly 1 (red dashed line in Fig. 2B, D, F) indicates that the predictor has no observed association on the odds of the event occurring.

The odds ratio of 3.55 (based on the estimated log odds of 1.267) for female mice vaccinated with BCG + ID93-GLA-SE 14 days post infection indicated a 3.55 times greater odds of T cell activation compared to the saline group at baseline (Fig. 2B), highlighting the effect of this immunization regimen on T cell activation during the early stages of infection. Similarly, female mice in the ID93-GLA-SE vaccination group at day 14 post infection had 2.8 times greater odds of T cell activation compared to the baseline group.

Conversely, our analysis showed that female mice given ID93-GLA-SE had an odds ratio of 0.4 in the predicted proportion of B cells, suggesting a decreased likelihood of increased B cell proportions associated with this specific treatment 14 days post infection compared to the baseline group (Fig. 2F). Additionally, males given saline showed a 0.23 decreased odds for B cells within the lungs 14 days post infection compared to saline females. Odds ratios for dendritic and natural killer cells are available in (Supplementary Fig. 2). Overall, these estimated effects and odds ratios provide insights into the strength and direction of associations between variables allowing us to assess the multivariable impact on host immune responses.
Probability of immune phenotypes in the lung during Mtb infection

Given the inherent complexity of incorporating interaction terms into our model, evaluation of overall patterns and associations from odds ratios can be challenging. For example, the previous results focus on female mice at day 14 as this is the baseline group and limits the interpretation as it allows comparisons only with the baseline group. Instead, we can translate estimates from the model into expected probabilities or "predictions" for each combination of vaccination group, days post infection, and sex.

In our framework, we employed predictand ggpredictfunctions in R to generate probabilities of key immune responses. By using variables "group", "day", and "sex" we can visualize how the probability of increased proportions of immune cells varies across different combinations of variables. It is important to note that prediction in the context of our GLM framework involves making inferences about the relationships of explanatory or "predictor" variables on the outcome of immune responses within our experiment and GLMs are unable to forecast future events or potential immune dynamics. Instead GLM allows for investigation into how changes in predictor variables are associated with changes in the outcome.
Probability of immune phenotypes in the lung during Mtb infection.

A-C Predicted probabilities of immune cell responses in the lung considering combinations of vaccination groups, days post-infection, and sex. A CD4+ CD44+, B CD8+, and) CD19+. All values were derived from the inverse of the logit function in our logistic regression model in R.

Our GLM framework revealed a higher overall probability of T cell activation for both female and male mice in the BCG-ID93-GLA-SE vaccination group. This group exhibited the highest probabilities of T cell activation when compared to the ID93-GLA-SE, BCG, and saline groups at both 14- and 90-days post-infection with an average probability of 13% on day 14 across both sexes (Fig. 3A), potentially indicating a BCG primed immune response. We observed that males vaccinated with ID93-GLA-SE alone did not increase observed proportions or probability of T cell activation when compared to BCG alone (Fig. 1B and Fig. 3A). However, females were predicted to respond better to ID93-GLA-SE vaccination compared to males alluding to the potential for sex to influence immune responses towards vaccination.

Notably, female mice exhibited a probability of 31% compared to males at 9% for developing robust B cell immune responses when considering sex alone at day 14 (Fig. 3C). This probability increased to 41% and 43% in females for days 56 and day 90 in the BCG + ID93-GLA-SE vaccinated group (Fig. 3C). Conversely, male mice in the BCG + ID93-GLA-SE group also had increased probabilities of B cell responses on days 56 and 90 but were still lower than females. Cytotoxic T cells did not demonstrate strong associations with group and day, however, sex might play a role in differential immune responses (Fig. 3B). Probabilities for dendritic and natural killer cells are available in (Supplementary Fig. 3). Based on the fitted model and predictor variables, these results demonstrate the probability of key immune responses, enabling the estimation of outcome probabilities across different combinations of explanatory variables as well as delineate which variables best explain the observed proportions of immune phenotypes.
Discussion

TB remains a significant global health concern, with millions of new cases and deaths annually, making effective vaccination strategies crucial. The BCG vaccine, though effective in childhood, has uncertain long-term efficacy, prompting the development of novel vaccine candidates and boosters such as ID93-GLA-SE. We emphasize the need for robust analytical tools to handle inherent variability in biological data as well as account for the multivariable influences on vaccine outcome:crucial for developing effective strategies against TB. While flow cytometry is essential for profiling immune responses within host tissues, biological diversity and technical variations present challenges including unequal data distribution. To address this, we used a GLM framework that can accommodate a variety of data types and can be extended towards more complex cases.

GLM offers several advantages over traditional statistical methods when analyzing proportional flow cytometry data. Firstly, it can accommodate non-normal distributions (including data describing counts and proportions) without the need for data transformations prior to fitting the model, as well as overdispersion commonly encountered in immunological data. Although data transformations allow for techniques like ANOVA on proportional data, the utility of GLMs allows for models appropriate for outcome data with a variety of data distributions, making it particularly suitable for analyzing diverse data types. As a result of these advantages, the use of GLMs has been steadily rising compared to ANOVA across fields including immunology and its implementation over methods that might require prior data transformations to meet normality assumptions has become highly encouraged. Secondly, GLM allows for the simultaneous consideration of categorical and continuous predictor variables, such as vaccination group, time post-infection, and sex, enabling a comprehensive assessment of the factors influencing vaccine-induced immune responses. GLM facilitates model parsimony, providing an approach to help strike a balance between simplicity and comprehensiveness by including only the variables that best explain the variability in the outcome. This approach ensures that the model remains interpretable while capturing the essential relationships between predictor variables and outcomes.

GLMs are now instrumental for modeling a variety of real-world biological and disease data, serving as a foundation for more complex and intricate models to predict likelihoods of disease outcomes in humans. The utility of the GLM framework also extends beyond the field of biology. In the realm of social sciences, researchers have implored the use of GLMs since the 1960's to facilitate the understanding of complex relationships between variables and predicted probabilities, and the application of regression models rather than the comparison of means continues to be encouraged. Psychologists find GLMs invaluable for studying behavior and cognition through complex experiments yielding non-normally distributed data. Environmental scientists also use GLMs to model diverse datasets ranging from wildlife population counts to pollution levels, accommodating the inherent variability and complexity within environmental data.

In our study, we demonstrate how our GLM framework enabled us to evaluate the probabilities of immune phenotypes present in the lungs of Mtb challenged mice and simulate outcome probabilities based on different combinations of predictor variables. The data restructuring into a GLM-compatible format marked the initiation of our framework, adopting an exploratory approach to grasp the distribution, variability, and proportions of immune responses within the dataset to identify potential trends and outliers for activated T cells, cytotoxic T cells, B cells, NK cells and dendritic cells. Notably, differences in lung proportions among vaccinated groups were observed for activated T cells and B cells, while cytotoxic T cell proportions seemed to be most associated with sex rather than vaccine. Observed proportions of immune populations provided insights into the distribution and variability across vaccinated groups, days post infection, and sex, setting a baseline for data quality and subsequent analyses.

Two GLMs were tested in this study, initially examining the effects of all possible combinations of "group" "day" and "sex" which became the expanded model. We then simplified the model and kept "sex" constant while evaluating the interactions between "group" and "day". Drop in deviance testing indicated a significant improvement in fit for the expanded model, supported by a greater proportion of explained deviance (57%) compared to the simpler model (43%). Overall, considering "sex" as an interaction term in the expanded model improved model variability and fit. Similar evaluations across immune populations favored the expanded model, leading to its adoption for all tested populations. The summary output of each model included coefficients, standard errors, t values, and non-adjusted p values, offering insight into predictor-outcome relationships.

Odds ratios with respect to cell mediated immunity indicated a considerable increase in the log-odds of T cell activation was observed in females vaccinated with BCG + ID93-GLA-SE 14 days post-infection. This increase was notable when compared to saline females 14 days post infection. This observation translates to a substantial increase in the odds (3.55 times higher) of T cell activation for females vaccinated with BCG + ID93-GLA-SE compared to saline. This demonstrates the impact of this regimen on immune responses during the initial stages of infection, indicating an overall increased likelihood of T cell activation in females vaccinated with BCG + ID93-GLA-SE at day 14 post-infection.

The use of predictive modeling within our framework allowed for the generation of probabilities of key immune responses, offering insights into the intricacies of immune responses when considering the interactions of group, day, and sex. Notably, higher probabilities of T cell activation were observed in both female and male mice vaccinated with BCG + ID93-GLA-SE on days 14 and 90 post infection. These data are of particular interest as they support the practice of BCG priming and boosting to induce stronger and more specific immune responses.

The role of sex in the risk of developing TB has been well documented, with males being twice as likely to develop the disease compared to females. It has also been observed that male and female immune systems respond differently to infections and immunizations, with females typically displaying more robust humoral responses than males. Our findings align with these studies when evaluating humoral immunity, as we observed clear differences between the sexes in B cell responses. Specifically, unvaccinated male mice had 0.23 reduced likelihood of B cell responses 14 days post-infection compared to unvaccinated females. This translates to a 31% probability for B cell responses in females, compared to a considerably lower 9% probability in males during the early infection period in unvaccinated animals. Furthermore, vaccination with BCG + ID93-GLA-SE was associated with increased probabilities of B cells in the infected lung of female mice at days 56 and 90 post infection compared to males. However, B cell responses were elevated compared to the baseline group in both sexes. Interestingly, we also observed T cell activation differences with respect to sex in the ID93-GLA-SE vaccination group at all timepoints, suggesting that females might have higher predispositions for T cell activation depending on vaccine regimen. It remains a possibility that therapies and vaccination for TB as well as other diseases may need to consider sex-specific, tolerance of infection, dosages, and correlates of protection.

Our study implements a GLM-based approach to deepen our understanding of vaccine efficacy and the dynamics of immune modulation in TB research. These data focused on results that showed strong effect sizes, biological plausibility, or aligned with prior literature or mechanistic expectations. As such we emphasize patterns and trends across related comparisons, rather than isolated statistically significant findings and acknowledge that without formal corrections, the false discovery rate may be elevated. We acknowledge there exists a limitation of sample size which was reduced to n = 4 after the addition of male mice in this pilot study. However, by incorporating a GLM framework and tightly controlling experimental variables such as genetically identical animals, consistent sample handling, synchronized time points, and fluorescence reference controls at each endpoint, we reduce biological and technical variability, increase GLM robustness, and navigate the limitations commonly associated with traditional statistical methods in real-world and immunological datasets. GLMs as a tool are also limited to the data being analyzed and are not appropriate for repeated measurements. While GLMs are flexible and widely recognized as efficient statistical tools across disciplines, instances where repeated measures are taken violate the assumption of independence. In such cases, Generalized Linear Mixed Models are better suited to account for the random effects of grouping and are effective at bringing independent datasets together to increase statistical power. This allows for hypotheses generated with a GLM to be further investigated with newly generated data. In the realm of immunology GLMs have been useful in drawing correlations between air quality and susceptibility to viral infection in children. In HIV and TB research, GLMs are utilized as a tool to associate relationships between host and disease.

In summary, we underscore the utility of GLM in analyzing high-dimensional flow cytometry data, which is crucial in evaluating the effectiveness of TB vaccine candidates and identifying the variables that influence their efficacy. By simultaneously considering multiple categorical and continuous variables, we provide a comprehensive understanding of how vaccination, days post infection, and sex shape vaccine-induced immune responses. In particular, we highlight the role of BCG priming and boosting regimens, as well as the influence of sex on vaccine efficacy. These insights are particularly significant as they can guide future research and development efforts in TB vaccine design, thereby playing a critical role in global TB control efforts.
Methods
Overview

We have created a statistical modeling approach for analyzing flow cytometry data to evaluate which factors are associated with immune responses in C57Bl/6 mice post-vaccination with Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG), ID93-GLA-SE, or BCG + ID93-GLA-SE, followed by Mtb infection. All data was acquired through high-dimensional flow cytometry and followed up by data processing in R to ensure compatibility with statistical analysis.
GLM framework workflow.

Our computational framework is comprised of four sequential data analysis steps which include, (1) Data acquisition from high dimensional flow cytometry and analysis software. (2) Initial data processing and exploration/visualization. (3) Logistical modeling withing the GLM framework. (4) Visualization of computed probabilities of outcomes based on variable interactions.

Within the GLM framework, the main effects of vaccination group, days post-infection, and sex on immune cell proportions are evaluated. Validation and interpretation of the model are facilitated through data visualization to understand their influence on immune modulation and probabilities of immune phenotypes present in the lungs. (Fig. 4) provides a graphical summary of the key steps in this framework.
Study design

Experimental pilot data generated for this analysis originate from female and male C57Bl/6 mice and have not been published before. Mice were procured from Jackson Laboratories and housed in a BSL-3 facility at Colorado State University. After an acclimatization period in the BSL-3, 6-week-old adult mice were randomly assigned to groups and vaccinated intradermally with saline, ID93-GLA-SE, or 1 x 105 CFU of BCG followed by intramuscular boosting with saline or ID93-GLA-SE 120- and 176-days post BCG vaccination. Mice were thereafter infected with Mtb Erdman. Mtb Erdman and BCG Pasteur strains were cultured as previously stated. Low-dose Mtb aerosol infections were performed with ~50-60 CFU deposited in the lungs of each mouse. At days 14, 56, and 90 post Mtb infection, female and male mice were euthanized via CO2 asphyxiation, after which lungs were harvested, and lung cells were processed into single-cell suspensions and stained for multispectral flow cytometry using a 19-color fluorochrome panel (Supplementary Fig. 4). All mice were the same age at each experimental endpoint.
Data acquisition

The flow cytometry data used in this pilot study were acquired on a 4-laser Cytek Aurora spectral flow cytometer which recorded 80,000 events per sample after each endpoint. Additionally, single-color reference controls were used at each endpoint to mitigate potential batch effects arising from laser and/or detector fluctuations. Flow cytometry data were analyzed using our manual gating strategy in FlowJo  software version 10.8.0. Cell phenotypes are normalized to live leukocytes per our gating strategy. An example of activated T cell gating is provided (Supplementary Fig. 4).
Data pre-processing

Using the tidyr R package (v1.1.4; Wickham 2021), the "raw" dataset was initially removed of extra names, spaces, and symbols. For example, column names such as "Leukocytes/Single Cells/LIVE/CD3+/Q1: CD4-, CD8+ l Count" were simplified to "CD3+ CD4- CD8+". This becomes the "cleaned" data frame.

Here, column names are not yet variables themselves but are cell types/observations. To create a "tidy" data frame, the "cleaned" data frame was pivoted to a long rather than wide format, which created the new columns, "cell type" and "cell type count", for each mouse and day.

The plain text data file from FlowJo  was imported into R Statistical Software (v4.0.3; R Core Team 2020). The exported data contains column names which are lengthy, include symbols (/, :, \, l), as well as extra spaces, and quadrant names. This does not follow the format of tidy data, which is essential for effective data analysis and modeling. Tidy data is structured in a consistent format where each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each value is stored in its own cell. This standard format facilitates data manipulation, visualization, and analysis in R. Our framework therefore, incorporates the following steps to convert the output from the flow cytometer into the tidy data format:

In our framework, we are interested in binary outcomes:from a given parent population of cells, which cells are in each subset (for example, the proportion of live leukocytes that are CD8+). This outcome is best modeled by the logistic modeling format included within the larger GLM framework. In this format, terminology often involves conceptualizing outcomes as successes and failures out of a set of trials. Success typically refers to the occurrence of an event or outcome of interest, while failure represents the absence or non-occurrence of that event. This binary classification allows for the modeling of outcomes.

To ensure compatibility with the GLM framework, the tidy data frame was filtered and formatted to represent the concept of trials and successes. For instance, when considering the probability of a leukocyte being a CD8+ T cell as the outcome of interest, "live leukocytes" and "CD3+ CD4- CD8+ " T cells were identified as trials and successes:respectively:representing total live leukocyte counts and CD8+ T cell counts. Furthermore, the number of failures was calculated by subtracting successes from trials which allowed for computation of proportions of immune cell subsets under different conditions. This "GLM ready" data frame, along with data frame pre-processing procedures are outlined in (Supplementary Fig. 5).

Our statistical framework aimed to estimate the main effects and interactions of three variables ("group", "day", and "sex") on the outcome of immune phenotypes observed in the lungs. We used a sample data set consisting of 45 male and 43 female C57Bl/6 mice, distributed across four vaccination groups and three post-infection timepoints to demonstrate this framework (Supplementary Fig. 6). We analyzed the cell counts of parent immune cell populations and subsets of these populations. Given that our outcome of interest is binary, we used a GLM framework with a logit link function. This allowed us to determine the relationship between the likelihood of cells in a parent population belonging to a specific subset and the predictor variables mentioned above. To accommodate for overdispersion:or excess variability:which arises when the variability in the data exceeds what can be assumed in the model, we employed a quasibinomial family using the glmbase R function. Overdispersion can be determined via the dispersion parameter output after the quasibinomial model has been fit. Values significantly greater than 1 indicate overdispersion and should be modeled with the quasibinomial family as models with very high variability can lead to inflated test statistics such as p values that are estimated to be smaller than the data supports.
Model parsimony

When considering GLM analysis, it is important to strike a balance between simplicity and effectiveness. A parsimonious model achieves this balance by including only the variables that best explain the variation in the outcome. By keeping the model simple, we make it easier to interpret the relationships between predictor variables and outcomes and in some cases, gain statistical power given the nature of the data and scientific inquiry. The previous model considered the three-way interactions between our predicting variables ("group", "day", and "sex"). Simplification of the model in our framework meant reducing the number of interactions. In this scenario, we explore holding "sex" as a constant across different levels of "group" and "day". Model fit diagnostics and choosing a model

To determine the best model fit, we applied an analysis of deviance to both the expanded and parsimonious models. In R, ANOVA for GLMs uses a likelihood ratio test to compare nested models, evaluating if a smaller model fits the data with similar quality. This method assesses predictor importance by quantifying the difference between models. We used the anova base function in R which performs a likelihood ratio test to compare the deviance (or likelihoods) between models. This function provides residual degrees of freedom, residual deviance, change in deviance, and associated p values. A p value (p < 0.05) indicates a significant difference between the two models in terms model fit. In this case, the model of choice would be the one with the best fit.

Separately we completed sensitivity testing of the GLM framework, applying an outlier and influence analysis using Cook's distance (adapted for GLM). Cook's distance is a well-established tool to identify influential data points that have a disproportionate impact on the GLM results. Here, we assess both leverage (how extreme an observation's predictor values are) and residual size (how far an observation's outcome is from the model's prediction). Briefly, we computed Cook's distance to flag potential outliers and understand the influence, leverage, and residual nature of those flagged points on the fitted model. This led us to identify several potentially influential data points in each immune population tested. We then identified the highest Cook's distance. For example, observation 34 (activated T cells) was found to have the highest Cook's distance (0.158), indicating may be most influential. Observation 34 also had the largest absolute residual. We also examined leverage which showed that observation 43 had the highest leverage. Importantly, observation 34 was the only sample flagged simultaneously for high influence and large residual (Supplementary Fig. 7).

Despite these findings, R's built-in influence.measures function did not flag any observations as influential by its default criteria, suggesting that while some data points are more extreme, they do not bias the model. We verified model stability by refitting the model after excluding the most influential observations and our conclusions remained qualitatively unchanged (this was also done for CD8 and CD19 populations) (Supplementary Fig. 7), as such we included these data points in our analysis. While a small number of observations exhibit higher-than-average influence or leverage, they do not substantially bias the model or its conclusions.
Residual analysis

We examined the performance of our selected GLM. Using the residuals  & fitted  functions in base R, we calculated deviance residuals and fitted values to evaluate the differences between observed and predicted values of our data. Following this, we created a residuals vs. fitted plot (Supplementary Fig. 8) to visualize the relationship between the residuals and predicted values. It is important to note that we did not observe any patterns or trends in the residuals that might indicate poor fit or overfitting. A well-fitted model would show no discernible pattern in the residuals.
Estimated coefficients and odds ratios

In our framework, we utilized the GLM framework to estimate coefficients that represent the association between predictor variables and the outcome. By exponentiating these estimated coefficients, we calculated the odds ratios, which can be interpreted as the odds of a successful outcome (immune phenotype) for a one-unit change in the predictor variable, while holding all other variables constant. For example, when using the vaccination group BCG + ID93-GLA-SE as the sole predictor variable, we set all values that are not BCG + ID93-GLA-SE to 0, effectively removing all interactions and testing the effectiveness of BCG + ID93-GLA-SE alone. This approach allowed us to calculate the main effect (or log-odds) of BCG + ID93-GLA-SE, providing a clearer picture of its impact on the odds of immune responses at baseline values for variables other than group.

We then exponentiate the log-odds to calculate the odds to provide a more intuitive understanding of the effect size and relative importance of each predictor variable in influencing the likelihood of a successful outcome.
Data visualization

All data visualization was completed in R with the use of ggplot2 R package (v1.2.3; Ludecke 2018) and ggeffects R package (v3.4.2; Wickham 2016) packages. To generate predictions, our framework defined a set of predictor terms ("day", "group", and "sex") and utilized the ggpredict function from the ggeffects package to generate predictions based on our fitted model. Additionally, we used the predict base R function to obtain probabilities directly from our model to aid in interpretation in the context of a model with interaction terms.

passages.text: Global variations in omega-3 fatty acid status and omega-6:omega-3 ratios: insights from > 500,000 whole-blood dried blood spot samples

Omega-3 (n-3) fatty acids are critical for human health, with the omega-6 (n-6) to n-3 fatty acid ratio and the omega-3 levels recognized as contributing to the risk of many chronic non-communicable diseases. Direct measurement of fatty acid levels in blood provides the most accurate assessment of fatty acid status and balance, with fingertip dried blood spot (DBS) analysis offering a practical and cost-effective assessment method. This study analyses more than 590,000 globally sourced DBS samples, providing fatty acid profiles in whole blood across diverse populations. Results reveal significant global and demographic disparities in n-3 levels and n-6:n-3 ratios, with suboptimal n-3 levels and imbalanced n-6:n-3 ratios prevalent worldwide. While the findings align with general trends reported in previous global mapping studies on omega-3 status in red blood cells (RBC), they are based on whole blood measurements and highlight the utility of DBS testing for large-scale monitoring. These results underscore the need to enhance n-3 fatty acid intakes to help mitigate multiple global health challenges and demonstrate the utility of fingertip DBS testing as a practical approach to design dietary interventions to promote overall well-being.
Introduction

Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA, 18:3 n-3) and linoleic acid (LA, 18:2 n-6) are essential for human health, as they serve as precursors to the longer-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) like arachidonic acid (AA, 20:4 n-6) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA, 20:5 n-3). The relative proportions of the n-6 and n-3 fatty acids in the body, captured in the n-6:n-3 ratio, are equally critical, as they determine the balance among proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory processes. This balance influences the production of lipid mediators, such as the resolvins and protectins derived from n-3 fatty acids, which exhibit pro resolving properties, while n-6 derivatives including certain prostaglandins and leukotrienes, exert a proinflammatory role. Understanding this interplay is essential for identifying dietary patterns and interventions that reduce disease risk and promote health.

The n-6:n-3 ratio also impacts the composition and functionality of cell membranes. At low dietary n-3 levels, the fatty acid intake has a significant influence on membrane composition. As n-3 levels increase beyond a certain threshold, membrane composition stabilizes, maintaining its integrity and functionality regardless of further dietary fluctuations. This stabilization is crucial, as low dietary n-3 levels leave membranes more vulnerable to functional imbalances, which can strongly impact cell signalling, gene expression, and the production of lipid mediators. When dietary fatty acid balance skews toward an elevated n-6:n-3 ratio, and the membrane n-3 levels are low, these processes promote a proinflammatory state that might exacerbate metabolic dysfunction.

Historically, diets rich in whole foods naturally provided a more balanced intake of n-6 and n-3 fatty acids. Modern dietary patterns have shifted toward an overconsumption of n-6-rich vegetable oils and processed foods, coupled with low intakes of n-3 fatty acids. This dietary shift has led to elevated n-6:n-3 ratios compared to the optimal range of 1-5:1 for health. The resulting imbalance drives chronic low-grade inflammation, impairing cellular function, and contributing to the rising prevalence of metabolic dysfunction and inflammatory diseases. In particular, a higher n-6:n-3 ratio has been associated with increased inflammation and a heightened risk of autoimmune diseases, cancer, cardiovascular disease (CVD), diabetes, and other chronic conditions.

Among n-3 fatty acids, the long-chain PUFAs EPA and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, 22:6 n-3) play particularly important roles in maintaining cardiovascular health, cognitive function, and modulation of inflammation, and are implicated in various neurological disorders. The impact of n-3 fatty acids depends not only on their absolute levels but also on their ability to counterbalance the high levels of n-6 fatty acids. These long-chain PUFAs influence the resolution of inflammation, the stabilization of neural membranes, and the modulation of oxidative stress. Importantly, studies assessing the effects of n-3 PUFAs must account for baseline blood levels and existing n-6:n-3 ratios, as these factors can strongly influence outcomes; Harris et al. showed that higher circulating n-3 PUFA levels correlate with a 15-18% reduction in all-cause mortality, particularly in individuals with initially low n-3 levels.

The literature on n-3 fatty acids, particularly EPA and DHA, is marked by notable discrepancies. While many studies and meta-analyses report protective cardiovascular or overall mortality benefits, several well-known trials and observational cohorts have not reproduced these findings. These inconsistencies arise from divergent study designs, differences in the methodologies used to assess n-3 fatty acid intake, and a frequent failure to account for baseline n-3 status or track improvements over time in intervention studies. Tools such as dietary surveys, are limited by recall bias and inaccuracies, highlighting the need for more objective measures. Analytical testing of biological samples offers direct insights into n-3 and n-6 fatty acid levels and consequently their potential physiological impacts; and is thus preferred for accurate evaluation of PUFA status. Importantly, it enables the determination of critical ratios, such as AA: EPA and total n-6:n-3, which are key indicators of fatty acid tissue balance and their physiological impacts, together with determination of n-3 levels (EPA + DHA), which reflects the biologically active omega-3 pool.

Dried blood spot (DBS) analysis has emerged as a practical non-invasive method for large-scale studies and global health monitoring. DBS allows for minimally invasive sample collection while providing data that correlates well with red blood cell (RBC) measures like the omega-3 index (O3I). Moreover, DBS offers a cost-effective and scalable solution, enabling its application in large populations and across diverse geographical regions. Whole-blood n-3 PUFA levels, measured using finger-prick DBS samples, include contributions from both plasma and RBCs and provide a comprehensive representation of fatty acid status. This measure correlates with tissue levels and health outcomes such as CVD risk.

The present study leverages what is believed to be the largest global database of n-3 levels and fatty acid profiles from DBS analysis, encompassing more than 590,000 samples. As noted, among the various fatty acids, EPA and DHA are the most biologically and clinically relevant omega-3s, and their combined concentration in blood (EPA + DHA) is widely used as a practical and validated marker of omega-3 status. In addition, the AA:EPA ratio is frequently used as an indicator of the balance between proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory lipid mediators, and the total n-6:n-3 ratio reflects broader dietary and metabolic PUFA patterns and is considered a marker of lipid balance at the populational level. Therefore, these three variables were selected for this study based on their established use in both clinical and epidemiological research, their functional relevance, and their interpretability in the context of nutritional surveillance and public health policy.

By mapping these levels across diverse regions and demographic groups, this study provides an unprecedented opportunity to evaluate geographic and demographic variations in fatty acid status. Additionally, the comparison of omega-3 supplement-users with non-users highlights the influence of supplementation on n-3 levels and fatty acid balance. By addressing both n-3 levels and n-6:n-3 imbalances, these findings have the potential to support public health strategies aimed at reducing the global burden of chronic diseases.
Materials and methods
Study design and data collection

This observational study employed a self-administered DBS fatty acid screening test analysed at the Vitas laboratory in Oslo, Norway. The home-based fingerstick collection method and test kits were distributed by Zinzino Operations (Sweden) through diverse channels, including health practitioners, therapists, web shops, and other sales outlets. By using DBS, broad participation is facilitated while minimizing the logistical challenges of traditional blood sampling, thereby enabling the collection of a large, international dataset.
Participant enrolment

Voluntary participants were recruited by filling in an online questionnaire, which gathered demographic data (age, sex, nationality, height, weight) and information on dietary supplement use. Those indicating use of omega-3 fatty acid supplements were asked to specify duration: "yes, for a little while", or "yes, for more than 120 days". Individuals who responded "no" or "yes, for a little while" were classified and stored in the dataset as "non-users of omega-3 supplements", whereas those responding "yes, for more than 120 days" were categorized as "users of omega-3 supplements". Details regarding the specific brands, dosages, or formulation of omega-3 products were not collected. The 120 day cut-off was chosen because it approximates the lifespan of RBCs. Since the measures are based on whole blood, which includes RBCs, this approach ensures that reported supplement use reflects a sufficient duration to affect RBC fatty acid composition (i.e., long-term omega-3 incorporation). Although the questionnaire distinguished between short- and long-term supplement use, short-term users were not retained as a separate category in the historical dataset used for this analysis.

To address concerns regarding the study's generalizability and to avoid potentially inflated n-3 levels from participants using the test kit provider's own supplements, individuals who reported consuming omega-3 supplements from Zinzino Operations (Sweden) were excluded from all analyses. This step was taken to minimize bias arising from brand-related supplementation patterns.
Inclusion criteria

A total of 595,480 fatty acid profiles were included in this study. Inclusion criteria were having answered all questions in the online questionnaire. Participants who answered "other" for sex and/or reported ages > 119 years were not included in the study.
Data management

Participants were informed about how their data would be managed and protected. They were required to actively consent to having their personal health data analysed by clicking an "I agree" button at the end of the questionnaire to be included in the study. Participants were also given instructions on how they could withdraw from the study and have their data deleted by sending an email including their personal test ID. The data presented in this study were collected during the period from 1st of April 2012 to 27th of September 2023. The study protocol was approved by the Joint Research Ethics Committee at the University of Central Lancashire, United Kingdom (HEALTH 01195).
DBS collection

Fatty acid profiles were obtained from whole-blood using DBS. DBS is a bio-sampling method in which capillary blood, obtained by a finger-prick lancet, is captured in spots on DBS collection cards. Participants received a pre-assembled sampling kit containing: (i) a single-use lancet, (ii) a Whatman 903 filter card, and (iii) and an aluminium-laminate pouch pre-loaded with calcium-chloride desiccant. After finger-prick collection, instructions were to allow the card to air-dry horizontally at room temperature for a minimum of 10 min before placing it into the aluminium bag and seal it for preservation until shipment to Vitas laboratory in Oslo, Norway for analysis. Samples were shipped at ambient temperature by regular post within the Nordic region or via consolidated express air transport (<= 48 h) from hubs at remote locations. The feasibility and general stability of self-sampled DBS specimens sent by mail have been previously demonstrated.
Fatty acid analyses of DBS

Fatty acid profiles obtained from DBS samples were analysed using established methods at the Vitas laboratory. Upon arrival at the laboratory, DBS samples were stored at 4  C prior to analysis within one week. The DBS samples were methylated with 0.5 M sodium methoxide for 20 min at 50  C to facilitate fatty acid methyl ester (FAME) formation. FAMEs were then extracted into hexane and analysed by gas chromatography-flame ionization detection (Agilent Technologies, 8890) with a TR-FAME column (length, 30 m; internal diameter, 0.25 mm; and film thickness, 0.25 mum; Thermo-Fisher Scientific).

Eleven fatty acids were identified as the major components of whole blood and quantified using gas chromatography. Each FAME was identified by comparing retention time to the external FAME reference standard (USP - FAME standard mixture, Merk). Fatty acid values are expressed as the percentage area of the total identified FAMEs, calculated as the sum of the 11 quantified fatty acids. The measured and identified fatty acids were: palmitic acid (PA, 16:0), stearic acid (SA, 18:0), oleic acid (OA, 18:1 n-9), LA, gamma-linolenic acid (GLA, 18:3 n-6), ALA, dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA, 20:3 n-6), AA, EPA, docosapentaenoic acid (DPA, 22:5 n-3), and DHA.

Whole blood n-3 fatty acid levels, herein referred to as "n-3 levels," were defined as the sum of EPA and DHA percentages, based on their established clinical relevance. The AA: EPA ratio was calculated using AA and EPA, and the total n-6:n-3 ratio was calculated as the sum of the measured n-6 fatty acids (LA, GLA, DGLA, AA) divided by the sum of the measured n-3 fatty acids (ALA, EPA, DPA, DHA).
Statistical analysis

A summary of the statistics is presented as mean or median values, as appropriate. Continuous data is expressed as mean +- standard deviation (SD) or standard error of mean (SEM), as specified, while categorical variables are expressed as proportions (%). Ratio data are expressed as median and the interquartile range (IQR) to account for potential skewness and ensure robust descriptive statistics. Confidence intervals (95% CI) are used for graphical representation of both mean and median values to illustrate variability and precision. Between-group differences were assessed using independent t tests or one-way ANOVA for unadjusted comparisons. For adjusted analyses, multiple linear regression models were used to examine the associations between omega-3 supplement use and n-3 levels, controlling for age, body mass index (BMI), and sex. Additionally, analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) was employed to compare n-3 levels across continents, with omega-3 supplement use and continent as fixed factors and age, BMI, and sex as covariates. Post-hoc comparisons were adjusted using Bonferroni correction. Effect sizes were calculated using Cohen's d, rank biserial correlation coefficients, or partial eta-square where appropriate. Significance was set to P < 0.05.

To ensure a representative dataset for country-level analysis, countries with fewer than 35 samples were excluded when presenting the mean n-3 levels, and median AA: EPA and total n-6:n-3 ratios in different countries. This decision was based on the Schuchardt et al. report, where the lowest number of participants included in any of their countries was 35, ensuring a reliable estimate of average levels. Additionally, colour-gradient maps were created to illustrate the global variations in n-3 levels and total n-6:n-3 ratio. For this visualization, countries with fewer than 35 samples were also excluded to minimize the impact of small sample sizes on the accuracy of the map representation. For continental group analysis, all countries were included regardless of their sample size to provide a comprehensive overview and to capture global trends. All statistical analyses were performed using JMP Pro (SAS Institute Inc., 1989-2019), IBM SPSS Statistics 28 and Microsoft Office Excel software. IBM SPSS Statistics 28 and Microsoft Office Excel were also used to create the figures.
Results
Demographic characteristics of the population

The mean age of the study participants was 47.3 +- 16.4 years. Only a small proportion of the participants were under the age of 20 (approximately 5%) or over the age of 80 (approximately 1.5%). Approximately 64% of the participants were females. Among adults over the age of 20 years, 48.5% were classified as "normal weight" based on their BMI. Although participants reported nationalities from all continents, 92.8% identified as European. Nationality was split into six regions, and European nationality was further split into four regions. A general linear model (GLM) univariate analysis revealed statistically significant differences in omega-3 supplement use across continents (F(6, 595582) = 1325.040, p < 0.001, eta2 = 0.001). However, the effect size was extremely small, indicating minimal practical variation in supplementation prevalence across continents. Within Europe, regional differences in supplement use were also significant (F(3, 552,913) = 2509.617, p < 0.001, eta2 = 0.013), but the effect size remained small.
Global n-3 PUFA status

An analysis of n-3 levels, AA: EPA, and total n-6:n-3 ratios across different continents and regions - without distinguishing between omega-3 supplement users and non-users - revealed notable geographical variations (Table 3). The lowest mean n-3 levels were observed in North America and Africa. These continents also exhibited the highest median AA: EPA and total n-6:n-3 ratios. Asia, Oceania, and Europe exhibited the highest mean n-3 levels, and within Europe, Northern Europe displayed the highest mean n-3 levels. Oceania, Asia, and South America showed the lowest median ratios of total n-6:n-3. Additionally, the lowest median ratios of AA: EPA were observed in Oceania, Europe, and Asia, and within Europe, the lowest median AA: EPA ratio was seen in Northern Europe. Overall, these data demonstrate notable differences in key biomarkers within the different continents and within European subregions.

Predictors of n-3 levels: multiple regression analysis

To explore the overall differences in n-3 levels in the study population, a multiple linear regression analysis was conducted, including supplement use, age, BMI, and sex as predictors (Table 9). N-3 levels were modelled as the outcome variable, with self-reported supplement use as the main predictor, adjusting for age, BMI, and sex. The regression model (R2 = 0.083) showed that omega-3 supplement use was the strongest predictor (beta = 0.220), followed by age (beta = 0.137) and BMI (beta = -0.111). Supplement users had 1.01% higher n-3 levels compared to non-users (95% CI: 0.997-1.020). Age and BMI explained less variation, while gender had minimal impact (beta = -0.059).

passages.text: Regional differences in n-3 levels by supplemental group

Among the 595,480 samples, the ANCOVA revealed significant continental differences in adjusted mean n-3 levels for both supplement users (F = 880.8, P < 0.001) and non-users (F = 642.3, P < 0.001), after controlling for age, BMI, and sex. (Fig. 3). Post-hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction revealed specific regional patterns: North America consistently showed significantly lower n-3 levels regardless of supplement use. Notably, Europe and Oceania showed no significant differences in either group (P = 1.000 for both), while Asia-Europe comparisons were significant among non-users (P < 0.001) but not among supplement users (P = 1.000). Asia also differed significantly from South America among non-users (P = 0.039). The partial eta-squared values indicated that continent explained 0.7% of variance in n-3 levels (partial eta2 = 0.007, P < 0.001), while supplement use showed no significant main effect (partial eta2 = 0.000, P = 0.001). The continent x supplement interaction was statistically significant but with negligible effect size (partial eta2 = 0.000, P = 0.001). Covariates collectively accounted for 9.3% of variance (adjusted R2 = 0.093), indicating that demographic factors substantially influence n-3 levels beyond geographic and supplementation effects.

Sex related differences in n-3 levels, AA: EPA, and total n-6:n-3 ratios

Next, sex-related differences in n-3 levels, AA: EPA ratio, and total n-6:n-3 ratio were examined. The analysis revealed a statistically significant difference in mean n-3 levels between females and males, albeit with a small effect size (Cohen's d = 0.184, Table 10). Moreover, females had a slightly lower median AA: EPA ratio than males, whereas the median total n-6:n-3 ratio was approximately the same. The rank-biserial correlations were negligible (r = 0.055 and r = 0.001), suggesting minimal differences between groups (Table 10).

Variations in n-3 levels and total n-6:n-3 ratios across age groups and BMI categories in omega-3-supplement users vs. non-users

Exploratory analyses were also conducted to assess how n-3 levels and total n-6:n-3 ratios varied across age groups and BMI categories, stratified by omega-3 supplement use. A significant increase in n-3 levels was seen among the different age groups (P < 0.0001) and increased with age, with a corresponding decrease in total n-6:n-3 ratio with age (Fig. 4A). Omega-3 supplement-users had on average, higher n-3 levels than non-supplement users, and 1.56% and 1.20%, respectively, of the variance in n-3 levels among them could be attributed to their age group according to eta-squared values from the analysis. Furthermore, non-supplement users had higher median total n-6:n-3 ratios than supplement users (Fig. 4B).

The relationship between n-3 levels and BMI (ages > 20 and < 80 years) was also examined using one-way ANOVA. The results revealed a significant effect of BMI on n-3 levels among both omega-3 supplement-users and non-users (P < 0.0001 for both). Eta-squared values indicated that BMI accounted for 1.6% and 0.95% of the variance in n-3 levels for omega-3 supplement-users and non-users, respectively (Fig. 5). Overweight and obese individuals had slightly lower mean n-3 levels compared to normal-weight individuals. Among omega-3 supplement-users, mean n-3 levels were 4.4% for overweight individuals and 4.1% for obese individuals, compared to 4.7% for those with normal weight. Similarly, among non-supplement users, mean n-3 levels were 3.4% for overweight individuals and 3.3% for obese individuals, compared to 3.6% for normal-weight individuals. Across all weight categories, omega-3 supplement-users consistently exhibited higher mean n-3 levels than non-users.
