Kharde et al. and Shinde et al. reported that the inclusion of spirulina in the broiler diet reduced feed intake, which is contrary to the findings of other investigators (Khan et al.; Abdelfatah et al.). However, this supports the findings of Spinola et al. that feeding 15% spirulina with and without commercial enzymes (pancreatin and lysozyme) to one-day-old male Ross 308 broilers for 35 days compared to the control treatment reduced feed intake and BWG by 29 and 38% and increased FCR by 10%. This corroborates the findings of Costa et al. on the adverse effect of supplementation of 15% spirulina with or without commercial enzymes on the growth performance of broilers. This implies that feeding 15% spirulina alone or in combination with commercial enzymes reduces growth performance metrics in broilers. Feeding a diet with up to 41% of SBM replaced by dried spirulina had no significant effect on growth metrics in broilers (Ross and Dominy). A study by Evans et al. shows that at higher inclusion rates (> 10%), the gelation of the proteins is reported, which leads to reduced amino acid digestibility and increased digesta viscosity. In a similar study, Pestana et al. found a 2 to 11% reduction in feed intake and BWG, and a 10% increment in FCR in broilers fed a diet containing 15% spirulina with or without commercial enzymes. The poor performance in broilers fed 15% spirulina with or without commercial enzymes could be linked to increased digesta viscosity due to resistant cell walls of spirulina that limit bioaccessibility and bioavailability of nutrients in broilers by preventing the target substrates from having access to endogenous enzymes (Jonhson and Gee). Overall, the variable growth performance data of broilers fed spirulina-based diets may be partly explained by chemical composition of spirulina, processing method, diet composition, and the level of spirulina in the diet (Bonos et al.; Rahim et al.). A previous study by Venkataraman et al. showed that the replacement of fish meal with up to 17% dried spirulina or GNC with up to 14% dried spirulina did not affect broiler performance. This confirmed the previous report that spirulina is a good source of digestible nutrients, including protein (Park et al.; Alwaleed et al.; Khan et al.), excellent amino acid profiles (Alwaleed et al.; Abdel-Moneim et al.; Mullenix et al.), and minerals (Alwaleed et al.; Kolluri et al.; Spinola et al.) and could be serve as feed supplement for humans and animals.
Blood characteristics

The feeding of varying levels of spirulina to broilers increased red blood cell (RBC) count, hemoglobin (Hgb), and packed cell volume (PCV) (Jamil et al.; Alwaleed et al.). Likewise, Zhang et al. reported that spirulina increased the concentrations of RBC, white blood cells (WBC), and Hgb, whereas Fathi et al. revealed that spirulina supplementation at the levels 0.03, 0.05, 0.07, and 0.09% had no significant effects on Hgb, PCV, RBC, and red cell indices [mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH), mean corpuscular volume), and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC)], monocytes and eosinophil counts in broilers. In a similar study, Zhang et al. found that spirulina increased the concentration of RBC, WBC, and Hgb in animals. Furthermore, Mariey et al. observed that dietary spirulina (0.3 mg/kg diet) increased WBC counts in broilers, while Fathi et al. found significantly increased WBC and lymphocyte counts and significantly reduced heterophils (H) / lymphocytes (L) ratio at 0.09% spirulina supplementation which could be due to the immunomodulatory effect of spirulina bioactive compounds (Khan et al.). The improvement effect of spirulina on RBC may be partially related to its high concentrations of iron (90 mg/100 g) and B-complex vitamins, especially niacin, riboflavin, folic acid, and pantothenic acid, which help in the rapid formation of RBCs (Nasirian et al.; Spinola et al.). Furthermore, spirulina contains antioxidant compounds that assist in protecting RBC and other blood cellular components from oxidative stress. In contrast, Sugiharto et al. and Alwaleed et al. indicated that spirulina reduced WBC counts and aspects of differential WBC. These findings were at variance with the findings of Jamil et al. and Lokapirnasari et al. that spirulina increased WBC levels in broilers. This observation may be ascribed to several factors such as the growth condition of spirulina, its chemical composition, the level added to the diet, and the age of broilers used for the study.

Blood chemistry parameters of broilers were influenced by dietary spirulina supplementation (Hajati and Zaghari; Alwaleed et al.). Blood proteins reflect the formation of proteins in the liver, which may be related to broilers' growth performance and health status (Limdi and Hyde). A study by Alwaleed et al. revealed that spirulina inclusion at 0.5 and 1.0% increased the concentrations of total protein in broilers while serum albumin concentrations were increased at 0.5% of spirulina supplementation. This suggests the high quality of protein in spirulina-based diets (Liestianty et al.; AlFadhly et al.). Fathi et al. noticed significantly increased serum globulin values in broilers offered 0.03 to 0.09% spirulina for 38 days but did not influence total protein and albumin levels. Pestana et al. reported that broilers fed 15% spirulina + 0.005% enzyme had significantly reduced serum uric acid levels, implying that spirulina improved nitrogen utilization in broilers, hence leading to reduced protein degradation (Metayer et al.). Hepatic markers, including alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) are important indices used to assess liver function in farm animals (Ogbuewu et al.). Serum ALT and AST levels were reduced at high supplementation levels of spirulina (0.07 and 0.09%) in broilers (Fathi et al.), indicating that incorporation of spirulina to broiler diets did not compromise the normal function of the liver in broilers. This agrees with the results of Pestana et al..

The reduction effects of spirulina supplementation levels on lipid profiles, including total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), high-density lipoprotein (HDL), and very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) in broilers have been demonstrated (Zeweil et al.; Abd El-Hady and El-Ghalid; Alwaleed et al.). The potential of spirulina to lower the lipid profiles of broilers that received spirulina-based diets at 0.5 and 1.0% (Alwaleed et al.), 0.3 and 0.6% (Abd El-Hady and El-Ghalid) and 0.05, 0.07, and 0.09% (Fathi et al.) may reflect the ability of spirulina to inhibit the formation of cholesterol in the liver and its subsequent absorption from the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) of broilers (Mariey et al.; Spinola et al.). The high level of PUFA in spirulina may help to reduce the serum lipid profiles of broilers (Hajati and Zaghari). The hypolipidemic and hypocholesterolemic action of spirulina may also be related to the presence of phenolic compounds and C-phycocyanin, which inhibits the activity of fat-digesting enzymes in the chicken gut (Deng and Chow).
Immune functions

Khan et al. used 120-day-old male broiler chicks (Arbor Acres) which were randomly distributed into four groups of 30 broiler chicks each, with each group further allotted into three replicates of 10 broilers each. Group 1 had no spirulina (control 1), while Groups 2-4 received a basal diet supplemented with spirulina at 0.1, 0.15 and 0.2%, respectively. Results indicate that broilers on spirulina supplementation had better immune responses than the control. Based on the findings of Khan et al., spirulina supplementation at 0.1-0.2% supported immune functions in broilers. These findings are consistent with the work of Yusuf et al., who discovered that the replacement of subtherapeutic levels of antibiotic growth promoters with spirulina improved immune functions in broilers. Studies have shown that spirulina supplementation is an excellent source of important nutrients that may improve immune functions in broilers (Velten et al.; Spinola et al.). Lysine, an EAA found in high levels in spirulina aid in the generation of cytokines and the proliferation of lymphocytes, resulting in improved immune systems in the face of ailments (Nasr et al.). This inference was supported by Abdelfatah et al., who demonstrated that supplementation of spirulina to broiler rations at 0.1-0.5% improved the gut barrier function as shown by an increase in the expression of intestinal fatty acid-binding protein 2 (FABP2) that is charged with modulation of cell growth and proliferation.
Antioxidative biomarkers

Pestana et al. noticed increased antioxidative enzyme capacity in broilers fed 15% spirulina with or without enzyme supplementation, which could be attributed to antioxidant components in spirulina, including sulfated polysaccharides, carotenoids, chlorophyll, phycocyanin, tocopherol, ascorbic acid, and phenolic acid (Kolluri et al.; Spinola et al.). Research showed that broilers fed 0.1-0.5% spirulina exceeded the control treatment in terms of glutathione peroxidase (GPx), superoxide dismutase (SOD), total antioxidant capacity (TAC), and catalase levels. The GPx and SOD act as free radical scavengers within the cells (Ighodaro and Akinloye). The inclusion of spirulina in the diets ofbirds has been discovered to alter their redox status; for instance, Park et al. reported a progressive increase in GPx and SOD levels and decreased malondialdehyde (MDA) as spirulina levels increased from 0.25 to 1%. This observation was justified by the high content of antioxidant compound (C-phycocyanin) in spirulina (Spinola et al.), which is 16 times more effective than Trolox (a vitamin E analog) and 20 times more active than ascorbic acid (Romay and Gonzalez). Numerous phenolic compounds (e.g., chlorogenic, salicylic, caffeic acids, trans-cinnamic, quinic, and synaptic) in spirulina may also add to its antioxidant activity, individually or mixed.
Intestinal microbiota composition

In a study by Jeong and Kim, it was observed that intestinal microbial ecology correlates with high productivity and efficient feed conversion in broilers. Research by Abdelfatah et al. indicated that spirulina (0.1, 0.3, and 0.5%) increased the cecal Lactobacillus population in a dose-dependent manner whereas the coliform population was increased at 0.3% and 0.5% supplementation levels. In a study with animals other than broilers, spirulina reduced ileal E. coli count but did not influence lactobacillus counts (Hajati et al.). In contrast, others (Shanmugapriya et al.; Fathi et al.; Park et al.) found that spirulina increased the intestinal lactic acid bacteria (LAB) counts and decreased E. coli counts but had no effect on coliform count. The antibacterial effect of spirulina may partly be attributed to the activity of phenols and other bioactive compounds present in spirulina (Pradhan et al.). In vitro studies revealed that spirulina extracts inhibit the proliferation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphyloccocus aureus, Klebsiella pneumonia, E. coli, Salmonella Typhi, Candida albicans and E. coli, (Kaushik and Chauhan; El-Baz et al.; Shao et al.) while promoting the growth of LAB (Bhowmik et al.).

Alwaleed et al. found that supplementation of 0.5 and 1.0% of spirulina in a broiler diet decreased the population of ileocecal E. coli compared to broilers without spirulina supplementation. This result supports the findings of Shanmugapriya et al., who reported a decreased E. coli count in broilers fed a diet having 1% spirulina. In a study other than broilers, Yusuf et al. found reduced ileocecal coliform count in quails fed with 2% spirulina. Reduced intestinal counts of E. coli or S. aureus have been demonstrated in broilers on dietary spirulina supplementation (Kaushik and Chauhan; Nuhu et al.). These antimicrobial effects could be attributed to its rich concentrations of C-phycocyanin, sulfonated polysaccharides, tocopherols, and fatty acids (El-Sheekh et al.).
Intestinal morphology

The gut acts as a selective barrier, absorbing nutrients and rejecting toxins and pathogens (Sharma et al.; Pastorelli et al.). Thus, maintaining a strong intestinal barrier is critical for the welfare of animals (Jeon et al.). A weakened gut barrier encourages the passage of harmful substances, activating both the innate and adaptive immune systems (Senior et al.). The beneficial effects of spirulina on gut morphology and absorptive capacity of villi in broilers have been demonstrated in the literature (Shanmugapriya et al.; Yusuf et al.; Khan et al.). Spirulina is reported to enhance the proliferation of gut lactobacilli in broilers (Shanmugapriya et al.) and quails (Yusuf et al.). This finding agrees with Khan et al., who demonstrated improved gut morphology and absorptive capacity of villi in male Arbor Acres broilers fed a basal diet supplemented with 0.15 and 0.2% spirulina powder. The enhanced absorptive capacity of villi may be related to spirulina's biological effects, which include antioxidant, immunomodulatory, and antibacterial activities. Based on the above findings, it is possible to conclude that spirulina, when included in the right quantity in broiler diets, might enhance the intestinal villi parameters, perhaps leading to improved BWG and FCR.
Carcass traits, internal organs, and meat quality

The addition of spirulina at 0.15 and 0.2% to the diet of broilers increased the dressing percentage (DP) by 3.0 and 7.0% respectively (Khan et al.). Similarly, Alwaleed et al. reported increased carcass traits in broilers fed 0.1% spirulina. This finding is consistent with the results of Kaoud, who noticed that spirulina supplementation at 0.01% increased DP, liver, and gizzard weights in male Hubbard broilers, but had no significant influence on thymus and bursa weights. These suggest that spirulina-supplemented diets are superior to the control diet. It is evident from the findings of Abdelfatah et al. that the bursa, breast weights, and DP were higher in broilers fed 0.5% spirulina compared to those on 0, 0.1, and 0.3% spirulina supplementation. This is consistent with the results of Fathi et al. and Attia et al. that spirulina increased the weights of lymphoid organs in broilers exposed to heat stress conditions. The increased weight of lymphoid organs on spirulina supplementation suggests that spirulina improves immune functions in broilers. Khan et al. indicated that spirulina supplementation enhanced aspects of carcass traits and reduced abdominal fat (AF) content in broilers as documented by other investigatorss (Fathi et al.; Moustafa et al.). Similarly, Kaoud et al. found higher carcass yield, cut part weight (breast), and bursa weight in the spirulina treatment groups than in the control group. The improved carcass metrics (AF, DP, and breast muscle) can be related to spirulina's excellent essential amino acid profile, which includes lysine and methionine. This shows that for enhanced DP and breast muscle weight, spirulina which is high in lysine, required for protein synthesis and muscle deposition, should be added to broiler rations in the right amount. In converse, Cheong et al. found no effects of incorporating about 8% spirulina in quail diets on the carcass and breast weights. To date, the exact reasons for the divergent results are not well known, but genetic differences, the composition of spirulina, and the quantity of spirulina added to the feed may explain the differences.

The color of raw meat is an essential quality attribute for the selection of meat by the consumer (Fletcher). Chicken meat color is affected by nutrition and environmental variables (Venkataraman et al.; Toyomizu et al.). Spectrocolorimetric analyses indicated that supplementation of spirulina at a level between 4 and 8% in the diets of broilers aged from 21 to 37 days resulted in the orange-yellow color of meat compared to the control which was pale yellow (Toyomizu et al.). The authors also observed that the orange-yellow color did not change as levels of dried spirulina increased from 4 to 8% in the feed. This agrees with the earlier reports by Venkataraman et al. that spirulina improved the color of thigh, skin, and breast muscles in broilers. The high carotenoid (beta-carotene) and zeaxanthin pigments in spirulina could explain the improved orange-yellow color in broilers offered 4 and 8% spirulina (Spinola et al.). Another possible mechanism via which the meat color could increase in broilers offered spirulina may be related to increased myoglobin or iron levels in the meat due to the high levels of iron in spirulina (Spinola et al.). This implies that spirulina can be added to the broiler diet to enhance chicken meat color.

Based on the classification of the Food Advisory Committee, thigh and breast muscles are recognized as lean meats because of their low-fat content, which is usually less than 5%. Pestana et al.; Spinola et al. discovered that total lipids in breast and thigh meats of broilers fed 15% spirulina with or without commercial enzymes satisfied the criterion of the Food Advisory Committee. These findings are consistent with the values reported for thigh and breast meat by Ribeiro et al.. Studies by Pestana et al.; Spinola et al. show that spirulina reduced the cholesterol content of thigh and breast meats in broilers. The authors also reported that the predominant SFA in the thigh and breast meat of broilers fed spirulina-based diets were palmitic and stearic acids. Palmitoleic and oleic acid were the predominant monounsaturated fatty acids, whereas linoleic acid and arachidonic acid were the most abundant PUFA. This aligns with reports of Tokusoglu and Unal; Park et al. that spirulina is rich in oleic acid, linoleic acid, palmitic acid, stearic acid, and gamma-linoleic acid. The level of arachidonic acid was higher in breast muscles of broilers fed 15% spirulina with or without enzymes (Pestana et al.), which might be attributed to the conversion of linoleic acid, which is the dietary precursor for arachidonic acid (Martins et al.).

Minerals play an important part in several physiological processes in the animal's body (Schaible). A study by Spinola et al. found that the addition of spirulina to the broiler ration had no effect on macro-mineral levels in breast meat, but did reduce the magnesium and potassium levels in thigh meat. The authors also noticed that 15% spirulina raised the sodium content and reduced the zinc level in both thigh and breast meat. The increased digesta viscosity in broilers fed 15% spirulina alone or with blends of commercial enzymes (Pestana et al.) may impair the absorption of magnesium, potassium, and zinc from the gastrointestinal tracts.
Economics of production

Khan et al. discovered that broilers fed 0% spirulina (control) had lower total costs than those fed 0.1-0.2% spirulina. The authors also found that groups fed 0.1-0.2% spirulina had better gross return per bird and net return than the control group. In a similar feeding trial, Abd El-Hady and El-Ghalid reported that spirulina supplementation at 0.3 and 0.6% reduced total feed cost by 10 and 6%, respectively compared to the control. In addition, relative economic efficiency (REE) increased by 19 and 27% in groups offered spirulina at 0.3 and 0.6%, respectively compared to the control group (Abd El-Hady and El-Ghalid. Fathi et al. found higher total revenue, net revenue, and REE in broilers that received spirulina at 0.03 to 0.09% compared to the group without spirulina treatment. These findings confirmed the work of Kaoud and Mariey et al. who discovered that supplementation of up to 0.6% broiler feed resulted in increased economic efficiency in broiler production. Swati et al. revealed the addition of low levels of spirulina to broiler diets resulted in enhanced performance, however, it was observed that supplementation of spirulina at 5% alone or in combination with commercial enzymes is not economically feasible and can lead to a higher level of economic loss compared to the control group offered diet without spirulina and commercial enzymes.
Conclusion and future research directions

This review shows that spirulina is an excellent source of nutrients, including proteins, vitamins (B-complex vitamins, tocopherols, ascorbic acids), pigments (phycocyanin, chlorophyll, and carotenoids), minerals (iron, calcium, phosphorus, and potassium) and PUFA. Additionally, spirulina is also a rich source of protein and EAA when compared to conventional vegetable protein such as soybean meal, the main protein source in broiler diets. Research also revealed that spirulina is high in chlorophyll, carotenoids, and phycocyanins, which give spirulina its unique blue-green coloration. The rich nutrient content and pigmentations of spirulina may be responsible for its several pharmacological properties, including antimicrobial, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory effects.

This review demonstrates that the addition of 0.03-6.0% spirulina to the diets of broilers improved growth performance without adverse consequences on gut microbiota composition, gut morphology, blood characteristics, lipid profiles, antioxidative enzyme status, immune functions, internal organ, carcass traits, and meat quality. However, the introduction of high levels of spirulina (10-15%) alone or in combination with commercial enzymes into the diets of broilers reduced growth performance. The inclusion of high levels of spirulina in the diets of broilers increased digesta viscosity that tends to limit bioaccessibility and bioavailability of nutrients, which could explain the poor growth performance. The application of enzyme technology did not solve the problem of increased digesta viscosity, implying that a blend of other treatment methods such as enzyme and mechanical pre-treatments may be useful. In addition, the mechanisms underlying the poor growth performance of broilers fed high levels of spirulina with or without commercial enzymes is not clear and warrant further research. Further research is also required to ascertain the inclusion levels of spirulina that optimize broiler performance using a quadratic optimization model. There are also scanty published studies on immune functions, antioxidative biomarkers, intestinal morphology, and economics of production of broilers fed spirulina-supplemented diets, as a result, more research is needed in this direction.

This review revealed that supplementation of high levels of spirulina enhanced the breast and thigh meat color of broilers. Future research should focus on understanding the mechanisms involved in the meat color of broiler offered spirulina as it may yield new insights into practical applications for not only improving meat quality but also maintaining color uniformity in general meat or broiler meat marketing. This review showed that higher dietary spirulina levels reduced the content of magnesium and potassium in thigh meat while increasing the sodium and decreasing the zinc level in both thigh and breast meat. The reported decrease in the zinc level of both breast and thigh meat in broilers fed spirulina-based diets, poses a major concern for the nutritional quality of spirulina and calls for the enrichment of spirulina-based diets with zinc or cultivation of zinc-enriched spirulina. Furthermore, long-term trials should look into the potential health effects of eating broiler meat fed-spirulina diets, thereby providing a detailed understanding of its consequences for human health.

passages.text: Protease Domain Exosites Regulate Extravascular Binding of Factor IX(a)
Background:
Factor IX (FIX) is unique among the vitamin K dependent coagulation factors in that a substantial portion is bound to extravascular sites.
Objectives:
Determine the impact of exosites in the human FIX protease domain on clearance, tissue distribution, and activity in hemophilic mice.
Methods:

Human FIX(a) variants with protease domain substitutions in the antithrombin (R150A), heparin (K126A/K132A) and FIX Padua (R170A) exosites were evaluated in hemophilia B (zymogen) and A (protease) mice. Pharmacokinetic modeling of FIX(a) clearance, select tissue content and in vivo activity were determined.
Results:

FIX wild type (WT) demonstrated poor plasma recovery, biphasic clearance and heterogenous tissue binding. FIX WT was predominantly found in liver, followed by plasma, kidney, heart and brain. Equimolar FIX variants were similar except for FIX K126A/K132A, which demonstrated 2.3-fold higher plasma recovery and reduced liver content. FIXa WT was cleared more rapidly than zymogen, but also had poor recovery, biphasic clearance and heterogeneous tissue binding. FIXa-GGACK accelerated clearance from all compartments in the distribution phase but prolonged the terminal phase relative to FIXa. FIXa K126A/K132A, R150A and R170A demonstrated 2-3-fold higher plasma recovery than wild type, with reduced liver content for FIXa K126A/K132A. Despite reduced coagulant activity, FIX K126A/K132A and R150A demonstrated intact or enhanced potency relative to FIX WT in the saphenous vein bleeding and FeCl3-induced carotid artery occlusion models, while FIX R170A had enhanced potency in both models.
Conclusions:
Protease exosites regulate in vivo clearance, distribution, and FIX(a) activity. Human FIX(a) demonstrates extensive, tissue specific binding to extravascular sites.
Introduction:

Factor IX (FIX) is unique among the vitamin K dependent coagulation factors in that a substantial portion of the zymogen is bound to extravascular sites. Injection of saturating FIX in the CRM-negative hemophilia B mouse demonstrates that the extravascular compartment binds ~3-fold more FIX than present in plasma and this extravascular component contributes to in vivo hemostasis. The clinical relevance of the extravascular compartment is highlighted by the poor recovery of injected FIX in hemophilia B patients, which contrasts with the robust recovery of factor VII and X in respective factor-deficient patients. Repeat or continuous FIX infusion in hemophilia B patients results in a gradual increase in trough or steady state levels, respectively, consistent with saturation of extravascular binding. Similarly, the apparent volume of distribution for FIX is significantly larger than plasma, and the biphasic clearance of FIX in hemophilia B patients is consistent with a two-compartment pharmacokinetic model.

FIX binds reversibly to vascular endothelium and extravascular matrix, in part, mediated by the interaction of specific Gla domain residues with collagen IV. Human FIX K5A (legacy numbering), a variant with reduced collagen IV affinity, demonstrates enhanced plasma recovery and reduced volume of distribution in hemophilia B mice. Despite possessing relatively intact in vitro clotting activity and elevated plasma levels compared to wild type FIX, a "knock-in" mouse expressing the FIX K5A variant demonstrates a mild bleeding tendency, suggesting that collagen IV binding contributes to in vivo hemostatic function. FIX K5R, a variant with enhanced collagen IV affinity, demonstrates decreased plasma recovery and increased volume of distribution in hemophilia B mice, consistent with enhanced extravascular binding. Hemophilia B mice injected with a FIX K5R exhibit improved hemostasis 7 days post injection compared to FIX WT and K5A, despite plasma FIX levels <1% by 3 days.

In vivo extravascular binding of FIXa has not been similarly characterized, but interaction with collagen IV may also be relevant for protease distribution. Further, FX activation by the intrinsic tenase (FIXa-FVIIIa) complex and FIXa inactivation by antithrombin (AT) involve interaction with protease domain exosites. Based on their critical importance for substrate recognition and inhibition, we hypothesized that protease exosites impact the in vivo distribution and activity of FIX(a). To test this hypothesis, we employed the recombinant human FIX wild type (WT) and the variants K126A/K132A, R150A, and R170A (chymotrypsinogen numbering) in hemophilic mice (Fig S1). FIX K126A/K132A disrupts the heparin-binding exosite on the protease domain, which participates in direct inhibition of the FIXa-FVIIIa complex by glycosaminoglycans, acceleration of AT inhibition by unfractionated heparin, and stimulation of cofactor-dependent enhancement of protease catalysis. FIX R150A disrupts a key residue in the AT-binding exosite on the protease domain; reducing the rate of inhibition by AT in both the absence or presence of heparin pentasaccharide. Finally, FIX R170A, which demonstrates enhanced cofactor-dependent coagulant activity similar to the FIX Padua (R170L) variant, was included to assess the cofactor interactive site on the protease domain. The effect of these variants on the in vivo pharmacokinetics, tissue distribution, hemostatic and thrombogenic activities of human FIX(a) were examined.
Materials and Methods:
Materials:
Refer to Table S1 for information on Materials and Reagents.
Methods:
Mice strains:

Hemophilia B mice (HemB) Stock# 004303, Hemophilia A mice stock# 004424 (HemA) and C57Bl/6J wild type (WT) Stock# 000664 were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME, USA) and bred in-house. WT C57Bl/6J mice were control animals. Mice were aged 9-12 weeks for this study. All experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

Mice were anesthetized using isoflurane/O2 for all procedures. Blood samples were collected from the retro-orbital vein plexus using either heparin coated capillary tubes or 3.2% citrated sodium as the anti-coagulant. Plasma was isolated by centrifugation at 2000x g for 1 min, flash frozen and stored at -80  C until use.
Recombinant human FIX and FIXa variants:

Human FIX (rFIX) wild type (WT) and variants with alanine substitutions in the AT (R150A) and heparin-binding (K126A/K132A) exosites, and the mutated residue in FIX Padua (R170A) (chymotrypsinogen # system) were constructed, expressed, purified and quantitated as previously described. Mutagenesis primers are listed in Table S1. FIXa structure with overlay of binding sites, amino acid substitutions, and correlation between HGVS, legacy and chymotrypsinogen residue numbering is provided in Figure S1. See Supplemental Methods for details.
Factor IXa-GGACK:

FIXa was inactivated with Glu-Gly-Arg-chloromethyl ketone (GGACK from Prolytix) by incubation of FIXa with 12-fold excess GGACK at room temperature for 2 hrs in 20 mM HEPES, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 0.1% PEG-8000. Excess GGACK was removed by exhaustive dialysis against 20 mM HEPES, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 0.1% PEG-8000. Inactivated protease was quantitated by OD280-320nm.
Human specific FIX ELISA:

To determine plasma FIX levels, the ELISA was based on a modified Green Mountain Antibody (GMA) ELISA protocol using an affinity purified sheep anti-human FIX capture antibody (SAFIX-AP) from Affinity Biologicals. The detection antibody was SAFIX-AP biotinylated using the Abnova biotinylation kit per manufacturer instructions. This human FIX specific ELISA was employed for plasma samples from the pharmacokinetic studies, and subsequently modified to reduce background in the tissue lysates with adjustments in blocking buffer; washes, sample dilution and the biotinylated SAFIX-AP antibody step to include pre-incubation with streptavidin HRP and addition of a 6-fold excess of free biotin before addition to the plate (see Supplemental Methods).
Human Factor IX pharmacokinetics (PK) in the hemophilia B mouse:

Hemophilia B mice were injected in the tail vein with 85.6 mug/kg of FIX WT (~18 U/kg) or FIX variants. Serial retro-orbital blood samples were collected into heparinized capillary tubes between 2 min and 25 hr using brief anesthesia with isoflurane/O2 at each time point. Mouse plasma was isolated and FIX concentrations determined with the human specific FIX(a) ELISA using variant-specific standard curves. PK model building and evaluation was conducted using NONMEM Version 7 level 5 (NONMEM, ICON Development Solutions, Ellicott City, MD, USA), and followed standard model building approaches to define the structure, intersubject variability, and covariate dependence of the model. FIX concentrations were successfully modelled using a two-compartment biexponential model (see Supplemental Methods).
Human Factor IXa clearance in the hemophilia A mouse:

PK modeling of recombinant human FIXa clearance in the hemophilia A mouse was determined as above for the zymogen, with tail vein injection of a weight-based dose of 68.8 mug/kg FIXa WT (the molar equivalent of the zymogen dose) or FIXa variants. Serial retro-orbital blood samples were collected between 2 min and 3 hr as described above, except plain capillary tubes were used with 3.2% sodium citrate as the anti-coagulant. FIXa concentrations were determined with the human specific FIX(a) ELISA above using protease variant specific standard curves.
Analysis of Factor IX/IXa tissue content in hemophilia B/hemophilia A mice:

Hemophilia B mice were tail vein injected with 85.6 mug/kg FIX WT or FIX K126A/K132A. Similarly, hemophilia A mice were tail vein injected with an equimolar dose of 68.8 mug/kg FIXa WT, K126A/K132A, R150A, R170A, or FIXa-GGACK. At 5 min post-injection, mice were sacrificed following retro-orbital blood draw and organs (liver, kidneys, heart, and brain) were harvested, rinsed extensively in PBS, blot dried and organ weights recorded. Tissue lysates were prepared by addition of 200 mul lysis buffer (150 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris, pH 7.4, 1 mM EDTA, 0.1% SDS, 1% Triton-X-100, 1% NP-40 plus protease inhibitor cocktail) for every 70 mg of tissue followed by homogenization, clarification and freezing samples as described in Supplemental Methods. Lysate FIX(a) content was determined with the modified human specific FIX(a) ELISA using variant specific standard curves for both zymogen and protease. ELISA background was determined with identical tissue lysates prepared from saline-injected hemophilia B or A mice, respectively.
Saphenous vein bleeding model:
The saphenous vein bleeding model was performed as previously described with slight modification. See Supplemental Methods for details.
FeCl3-induced carotid artery occlusion model:
FeCl3-induced carotid artery occlusion model was performed as previously described with slight modifications. See Supplemental Methods for details.
Statistical Analysis:
A detailed description is provided in Supplemental Methods.
Results:
Recovery and clearance of human rFIX variants in hemophilia B mice.

Hemophilia B mice (23-28 g) were injected with human rFIX wild type (WT) or rFIX variants (N= 6-9 mice/variant). A biphasic elimination curve was observed, consistent with a two-compartment model for FIX distribution and clearance (Fig 1). Following IV administration of FIX WT, ~15% of the total FIX dose was recovered in the plasma at 2 min post-injection (Table S2). FIX R150A and R170A demonstrated similar recovery (16-17%) (Table S2). In contrast, FIX K126A/K132A demonstrated significantly enhanced recovery relative to FIX WT with ~35% zymogen in the plasma compartment. PK modeling of the FIX clearance data resulted in a two-compartment model that provided estimates of plasma clearance (CL1), central (V1) and peripheral (V2) compartment volumes, half-lives for redistribution (t1/2alpha) and elimination phases (t1/2beta) and Cmax (Table 1A). Notably, V1 was markedly higher than expected murine plasma volume (0.04 ml/gm), suggesting rapid binding of FIX within the vascular compartment. Likewise, V2 was markedly higher than the expected murine total body water (0.725 ml/gm), consistent with extensive FIX binding in the extravascular compartment. FIX K126A/K132A demonstrated a significant increase in Cmax and reductions in both V1 and V2 relative to FIX WT, whereas there were no significant differences for the FIX R150A and R170A variants (Table 1A). For additional details of PK modelling, see Table S3A.
Tissue distribution of human FIX wild type and K126A/K132A in the hemophilia B mouse.

Based on the enhanced recovery of FIX K126A/K132A relative to FIX WT in the plasma, zymogen tissue distribution was compared. Hemophilia B mice underwent tail vein injection with FIX WT or FIX K126A/K132A with blood collection and organ harvest (liver, kidneys, heart and brain) at 5 min post injection (n=8 mice/variant).

FIX tissue concentration was determined by total FIX (ng) present in lysate per organ weight (mg) (Fig 2A). FIX organ distribution was determined by the % total administered FIX dose present in each organ. (Fig 2B). Distribution in the plasma compartment was based on a murine plasma volume of 40 ml/kg body weight. FIX WT tissue concentration at 5 min post-injection was highest in the liver (0.78 ng/mg), followed by the kidney (0.08 ng/mg), heart (0.02 ng/mg) and brain (<0.01 ng/mg) (Fig 2A). The largest proportion of the total FIX WT dose was likewise in the liver (~48%), followed by plasma (11%), kidneys (1.3%), heart (0.14%) and brain (below detection) (Fig 2B). The tissue concentration of the FIX K126A/K132A variant at 5 min post-injection was also highest in the liver (0.56 ng/mg), followed by the kidney (0.11 ng/mg), heart (0.04 ng/mg) and brain (<0.01 ng/mg) (Fig 2A). The largest proportion of the FIX K126A/K132A dose at 5 min post-injection was in plasma (44%), followed by liver (34%), kidney (1.7%), heart (0.19%), and brain (below detection) (Fig 2B).

Determination of hemoglobin content in each tissue lysate allowed calculation of retained blood volume. Residual plasma volume was estimated using expected hematocrit and plasma FIX concentrations determined by ELISA were used to calculate the contribution of residual blood to total organ FIX content. These calculations suggested that <0.5 % of the liver FIX content was contributed by residual blood for FIX WT and K126A/K132A (Table S4A). Likewise, 1.0% of total kidney and 3.2% of total heart FIX WT content was contributed by residual blood. The total kidney and heart FIX K126A/K132A content contributed by residual blood was 2.3 % and 5.3%, respectively. The minimal contribution of residual blood to total FIX detected in the tissue lysates did not significantly impact conclusions regarding extravascular FIX distribution.
Recovery and clearance of human factor IXa (FIXa) variants in hemophilia A mice.

Preliminary experiments injecting human FIXa into the jugular vein of hemophilia B mice resulted in visible thrombi. To avoid FIXa consumption, distribution and clearance of human FIXa variants was examined in hemophilia A mice. Hemophilia A mice (20-25 g) were injected with recombinant FIXa variants (N=6-9 mice/variant), at an equimolar dose to the zymogen in Figure 1. FIXa WT clearance was substantially faster than zymogen but demonstrated similar poor recovery (~16% total dose) at 2 min (Table S2) and a biphasic clearance pattern (Fig 3). FIXa WT demonstrated a similar t1/2alpha (redistribution phase) to zymogen but the t1/2beta (elimination phase) was > 8-fold shorter (Table 1B). To evaluate the role of the FIXa active site, FIXa WT was modified with an irreversible chloromethyl ketone inhibitor (GGACK). Pairwise comparison of FIXa-GGACK with unmodified FIXa demonstrated similarly poor plasma recovery (~14%), 6-fold increase in V2, 2.8-fold shorter redistribution phase (t1/2alpha) and 3.8-fold prolongation of the elimination phase (t1/2beta) (Table S2, Fig 3 & Table 1B).

Human FIXa variants with reduced affinity for AT (R150A) or heparin (K126A/K132A) and the Padua-like protease (R170A), demonstrated enhanced plasma recovery relative to FIXa WT. FIXa R150A demonstrated ~31% recovery (~1.9-fold increase), FIXa K126A/K132A ~40% recovery (~2.5-fold increase) and FIXa R170A ~43% recovery (~2.7-fold increase) at 2 min post-injection (Table S2). FIXa K125A/K132A and R170A variants demonstrated significantly slower plasma clearance relative to FIXa WT with increased Cmax and reduced V1. FIXa R150A demonstrated similar trends but did not reach statistical significance (Fig 3 & Table 1B).
Tissue distribution of human FIXa variants in the hemophilia A mouse.

To evaluate the enhanced plasma recovery of the FIXa K126A/K132A, R150A and R170A variants and the altered clearance of FIXa-GGACK, protease tissue distribution was examined. Hemophilia A mice were injected with recombinant human FIXa variant (equimolar dose to zymogen), followed by blood and organ harvest at 5 min post-injection (n= 4-13 mice/variant). FIXa tissue concentration was determined by total FIXa (ng) present in lysate per organ weight (mg) (Fig 4A) and organ distribution was determined by % total administered FIXa dose present in each organ. (Fig 4B). FIXa WT tissue concentration at 5 min post-injection was highest in the liver (0.42 ng/mg), followed by kidney (0.12 ng/mg), heart (0.02 ng/mg) and brain (< 0.01 ng/mg) (Fig 4A). The largest portion of the total FIXa WT dose was in the liver (~23%), followed by plasma (17%), kidneys (2.4%), heart (0.2%) and brain (undetectable) (Fig 4B). Relative to wild type protease, FIXa K126A/K132A demonstrated significantly reduced liver concentration (0.26 ng/mg), and increased kidney concentration (0.22 ng/mg) (Fig 4A). FIXa R150A showed similar liver concentration (0.46 ng/mg) with > 2-fold higher concentration in the kidney (0.26 ng/mg) and heart (0.05 ng/mg) relative to FIXa WT. FIXa R170A demonstrated similar liver concentration (0.38 ng/mg), with modestly increased kidney (0.16 ng/mg) and heart (0.04 ng/mg) concentrations relative to wild type protease. FIXa-GGACK demonstrated reduced liver (0.25 ng/mg) and kidney concentrations (0.08 ng/mg) with similar heart concentration (0.03 ng/mg). All FIXa variants were undetectable (< 0.01 ng/mg) in the brain. In contrast to FIXa WT, the largest proportion of the FIXa K126A/K132A dose remained in the plasma (33%), with decreased liver (14%), increased kidneys (4.0%), and similar heart (0.2%) content to FIXa WT (Fig 4B). The largest proportion of FIXa R150A remained in the liver (28%), with relative increases in plasma (24%), kidneys (5.5%), and heart (0.4%) content. FIXa R170A demonstrated similar proportions in the plasma (24%) and liver (21%), followed by kidneys (3.4%), and heart (0.3%). FIXa-GGACK demonstrated the lowest proportion of detectable protease in the liver (14%), followed by plasma (5.3%), kidneys (1.6%), and heart (0.2%).
In vivo hemostatic activity of human FIX variants in hemophilia B mice.

The hemostatic activity of the human FIX variants was evaluated in the saphenous vein bleeding assay, with results expressed as the number of clots formed per 30 min. Hemophilia B male mice demonstrated no baseline hemostatic activity while wild type male and female C57Bl/6J mice demonstrated similar hemostatic activity (Fig 5A). Injection of rFIX WT into either hemizygous male or homozygous female hemophilia B mice demonstrated similar hemostatic activity (Fig 5A). Based on disease relevance and increased size of the male mice (enhanced consistency of vascular injury), comparisons between rFIX variants employed male hemophilia B mice. Injection of rFIX WT into male hemophilia B mice (N= 6-14 mice/dose) showed a dose dependent increase in hemostatic activity from 1.3 +- 0.5 to 16.5 +- 1.0 clots/30 min (mean +- S.E.M.), respectively (Fig 5B & Table S6). Injection of rFIX R150A (N= 6-9 mice/dose) likewise demonstrated a dose dependent increase in hemostatic activity from 3.4 +- 0.5 to 20.1 +- 1.8 mean clots/30 min with enhanced activity at low FIX doses compared to FIX WT. Injection of rFIX K126A/K132A (N= 7 mice/dose) showed a dose dependent increase in hemostatic activity from 2.1 +- 0.5 to 14.0 +- 0.6 mean clots/30 min similar to FIX WT. Finally, injection of rFIX R170A (N= 5-7 mice/dose) demonstrated a dose dependent increase from 6.4 +- 1.3 to 21.0 +- 2.1 mean clots/30 min, with enhanced activity at low FIX doses compared to FIX WT (Fig 5B). The FIX R170A response saturated by 57.1 mug/kg rFIX, suggesting that the in vivo hemostatic potency of this variant was 3-5-fold higher than FIX WT, consistent with its enhanced in vitro coagulant activity.
In vivo activity of human FIX variants in the carotid artery occlusion model in hemophilia B mice.

The thrombogenic activity of the human FIX variants was evaluated in the carotid artery occlusion model, measuring the time to complete occlusion (TTO). Saline-injected control C57Bl/6J wild type mice (5.8 +- 0.8 min) and hemophilia B mice (30.0 +- 0.08 min) demonstrated expected relative levels of thrombogenic activity (Fig 6A). Hemophilia B male mice were injected with human rFIX WT (N = 7-8 mice/dose). Vessel occlusion was not consistently observed for FIX WT at the 14.3 mug/kg (data not shown) or 28.5 mug/kg dose (>30 min), while the 57.1 mug/kg (12.7 +- 1.2 min) and 85.6 mug/kg (8.2 +- 0.6 min) doses progressively shortened the TTO (Fig 6A). FIX R150A (N = 5-7 mice/dose) similarly failed to consistently trigger vessel occlusion at the 28.5 mug/kg (>30 min) but shortened the TTO at 57.1 mug/kg (9.8 +- 1.4 min) and 85.6 mug/kg (8.6 +- 0.5 min) (Fig 6B & Table S7). FIX K126A/K132A (N= 6-7 mice/dose) inconsistently triggered vessel occlusion at the 14.3 mug/kg dose (26.0 +- 2.6 min) but demonstrated dose dependent shortening of the TTO at 28.5 mug/kg (10.3 +- 1.5 min), 57.1 mug/kg (8.0 +- 0.9 min) and 85.6 mug/kg (5.7 +- 0.8 min) with increased thrombogenic potency at lower FIX doses compared to FIX WT. Finally, FIX R170A (6-10 mice/dose) inconsistently triggered carotid occlusion at the 14.3 mug/kg dose (28.3 +- 1.8 min) but rapidly shortened the TTO compared to FIX WT at 28.5 mugkg (9.1 +- 1.4 min), 57.1 mug/kg (6.6 +- 1.2 min) and 85.6 mug/kg (5.8 +- 0.7 min). FIX R170A also demonstrated enhanced thrombogenic potency at lower doses compared to FIX WT.
Discussion:

The extensive pool of extravascular FIX is unique among circulating coagulation factors, and in particular, contrasts with homologs factor VII and X that possess identical domain structure. The collagen IV binding site, localized to the N-terminal Gla domain, has a major impact on the extravascular binding of FIX. The contribution of the C-terminal protease domain to the clearance, tissue distribution and in vivo activity of FIX(a) was examined here by disrupting the heparin (FIX K126A/K132A) and AT-binding (FIX R150A) exosites, and substituting the Padua-like mutation R170A. The results suggest that the heparin-binding exosite substantially contributes to extravascular binding of both zymogen and protease. In contrast, the AT-binding exosite and the Padua-like mutation selectively affect protease distribution. Further, the relative in vivo activity of FIX was enhanced by disruption of the regulatory AT and heparin binding exosites, and substitution of the Padua-like mutation.

Following IV injection in hemophilia B mice, FIX WT yielded poor plasma recovery, a biphasic clearance pattern, and PK modeling consistent with a 2-compartment model. The markedly increased central (V1) and peripheral (V2) distribution volumes are consistent with rapid intravascular binding and extensive extravascular binding of FIX, respectively. Heterogeneous tissue distribution of FIX was observed in the hemophilia B mouse, which may reflect both vascular density and the predominant endothelial type. The highest tissue concentration of FIX WT was in the liver, a large, highly vascular organ with dual blood supply (hepatic artery, portal vein), the latter characterized by sinusoidal endothelium. These results are consistent with initial biodistribution of radiolabeled human FIX in the mouse or pig produced recombinant human FIX in rats. Kidney, a highly vascular organ characterized by fenestrated endothelium (particularly in the glomeruli), demonstrated the second highest FIX tissue concentration. Cardiac muscle and particularly the brain demonstrated markedly lower FIX tissue concentrations. These organs are characterized by continuous endothelium, with the latter possessing additional components (astrocyte end-feet, microglial cells, pericytes) that contribute to the blood brain barrier. The lack of detectable extravascular FIX in the mouse brain is consistent with radiolabeled FIX distribution, and may be relevant to clinical observations such as the significantly higher rate of intracranial hemorrhage in hemophilia B relative to hemophilia A subjects.

Disruption of the AT-binding exosite (FIX R150A) or presence of the Padua-like mutation (FIX R170A) had no significant effect on FIX recovery or clearance, likely reflecting lack of availability for these binding sites in the zymogen. In contrast, disruption of the heparin-binding exosite (FIX K126A/K132A) significantly increased plasma recovery. and decreased predicted V1 and V2 volumes relative to FIX WT, suggesting both reduced intravascular and extravascular binding. Based on the expected perivascular location of extravascular FIX(a), tissue perfusion was avoided but mouse organs were extensively rinsed prior to lysate preparation. Residual blood estimated by lysate hemoglobin concentration demonstrated negligible contributions to the FIX tissue concentrations. Tissue lysates demonstrated a significant reduction in FIX K126A/K132A liver concentration compared to FIX WT, with redistribution predominantly to plasma and less so to the kidneys and heart. Thus, the heparin-binding exosite substantially contributes to both rapid intravascular binding (likely to endothelium) and extravascular binding of FIX, particularly in the liver.

FIXa WT similarly demonstrated poor recovery, biphasic clearance, heterogeneous tissue distribution and PK modeling consistent with a 2-compartment model in hemophilia A mice. The rapid clearance and marked shortening of t1/2beta (elimination phase) relative to FIX likely reflects AT inhibition and FIXa-AT clearance. Occupation of the FIXa active site by chloromethylketone inhibitor (FIXa-GGACK) induces conformational changes in the zymogen-like basal protease structure that were associated with t1/2alpha shortening, marked increase in V2 and t1/2beta prolongation. The former findings suggest enhanced binding to extravascular receptor(s), while t1/2beta prolongation reflects disruption of AT inhibition due to an unavailable active site. PK modeling suggested that disruption of the heparin exosite (K126A/K132A) slowed clearance, reduced intravascular protease binding (V1) and prolonged the elimination phase (t1/2beta). Likewise, the Padua-like variant (R170A) slowed clearance and reduced both intravascular (V1) and extravascular (V2) protease binding. Disruption of the AT binding site (R150A) demonstrated trends toward reduced intravascular and extravascular binding that did not reach statistical significance.

The majority of FIXa WT was initially found in the liver and plasma with substantially smaller amounts in the kidney, heart and brain. Comparison of liver content revealed that FIXa WT was only ~65% of zymogen on a molar basis, which may reflect competition with endogenous murine FIX in the hemophilia A mouse or differences in the genetic backgrounds of the mouse strains. Importantly, these results demonstrated that extravascular FIXa binding occurs in the presence of physiologic FIX levels. Disruption of the heparin-binding exosite (K126A/K132A) predominantly redistributed protease from liver to plasma, and to a lesser extent the kidney. FIXa R150A and R170A variants redistributed to the plasma, kidney and heart tissue, independent of liver content. FIXa R150A disrupts critical exosite interactions with heparin-activated AT, which may reduce binding to AT-heparan sulfate complexes on the endothelium and in the basement membrane. AT predominantly localizes to the subendothelial basement membrane (via heparan sulfate) in amounts that vary by tissue. Thus, defective interaction with AT-heparan sulfate complexes likely results in a widespread reduction in the vascular binding of FIXa R150A. The mechanism for FIXa R170A redistribution to plasma is unknown, but may impact the increased in vivo activity of this variant.

In vivo hemostatic (saphenous vein bleeding) and thrombogenic (carotid artery occlusion) properties of the FIX variants in hemophilia B mice demonstrated both discordant (K126A/K132A and R150A) and concordant (R170A) behavior with in vitro enzymatic and coagulant phenotypes. FIX WT demonstrated dose dependent hemostatic activity that reached a level similar to the wild type C57Bl/6J mouse. Disruption of the AT binding site (FIX R150A) enhanced hemostatic potency relative to FIX WT, despite reduced in vitro coagulant activity (~62%). Disruption of the heparin binding site (FIX K126A/K132A) resulted in similar in vivo hemostatic activity to FIX WT, despite substantially reduced in vitro coagulant activity (~21%). In contrast, the Padua-like substitution (FIX R170A) enhanced hemostatic potency relative to FIX WT with early saturation of the response, concordant with increased coagulant activity of this variant (260%). FIX WT and R150A demonstrated similar dose-dependent thrombogenic activity while FIX K126A/K132A and R170A demonstrated enhanced potency. FIX K126A/K132A and R150A were again discordant relative to in vitro coagulant activity, while the FIX R170A remained concordant with in vitro activity. The discordant in vivo activities of FIX R150A and K126A/K132A reflect the role of AT and heparin exosites in regulation of in vivo FIXa activity. Consistent with our results, the zymogen-like variant FIXa V16L demonstrates reduced AT inhibition and prolonged plasma half-life similar to FIXa R150A, with a more profound reduction in cofactor affinity and coagulant activity. Remarkably, FIX(a) V16L also demonstrates increased potency relative to FIX wild type in hemophilia B mouse injury models.

Limitations of this study include sampling from a small number of organs, ELISA detection limits, differing genetic backgrounds for hemophilia A and B mouse strains, and FIXa dosing that exceeds expected physiologic levels. Although cross-species protein-protein interactions may affect activity, human FIX(a) interactions with mouse proteins in the intrinsic tenase complex or AT are largely intact.

The hemophilia B mouse model suggests that FIX undergoes rapid intravascular binding and extensive extravascular binding that is mediated, at least in part, by C-terminal protease domain binding to heparan sulfate proteoglycans. Based on previous identification of the collagen IV binding site in the N-terminal Gla domain, these data suggest that FIX has extensive interactions with extracellular matrix (collagen IV and heparan sulfate proteoglycans) that span the length of the protein. As these protease domain variants do not substantially affect the FIX-collagen IV interaction (Fig S10), the possibility of additive or synergistic interactions between these binding sites deserves further study. In support of this concept, heterotypic supramolecular aggregates isolated from basement membrane demonstrate both the heparan sulfate-modified proteoglycan perlecan and collagen IV. Extravascular FIXa binding is similarly reflected in the recovery, clearance and tissue distribution of protease variants in the hemophilia A mouse. Although the in vitro plasma half-life of FIXa is remarkably prolonged (~41 min) and dependent on AT inhibition, the in vivo elimination half-life (t1/2beta) of FIXa WT was ~2-fold longer, likely reflecting protease diffusion back into the plasma from extravascular sites. Selective effect of the AT and cofactor binding variants on protease clearance and the reduced t1/2alpha for FIXa-GGACK, suggests that protease conformation is critical to extravascular distribution. FIX with enhanced collagen IV binding or administration of multiple daily doses of FIX results in accumulation of extravascular FIX and in vivo hemostatic activity despite undetectable plasma FIX levels. While TF-FVIIa at the site of vascular injury triggers the initiation phase of coagulation, FIX(a) bound at the injury site may enhance local thrombin generation in the propagation phase (Fig 7). As the hemophilia A mouse model suggests that an excess of FIXa binding sites exist, local accumulation of extravascular FIXa may represent a mechanism for tissue-specific thrombosis.

Mice underwent tail vein injection with 85.6 mug/kg rFIX and serial blood samples were obtained retro-orbitally between 2 min and 25 hrs as described in Methods. FIX concentration in isolated plasma samples was determined with the human FIX specific ELISA. The mean rFIX concentrations +- SEM versus time were plotted and initially fit to the equation for a 2 compartment model: [IX]t = [IX]max*(C1*e(-k1*t) + C2*e(-k2*t)),where [IX] = FIX concentration, t = time, C1 and C2 = beginning concentrations for initial and terminal phases, k1 and k2 = rate constants for initial and terminal elimination phases, respectively.

Hemophilia B mice (n= 8 mice per FIX variant) underwent tail vein injection of 85.6 mug/kg FIX WT or FIX K126A/K132A with harvest of blood and organs (liver, kidneys, brain and heart) at 5 min post injection. Plasma was isolated and tissue lysates prepared as described (see Methods) followed by determination of FIX content in plasma and tissue lysates using the modified human FIX ELISA with variant-specific standard curves. The FIX tissue concentration was expressed as total FIX (ng) present in lysate per organ weight (mg) (Panel A). FIX organ distribution was determined by the % of the total administered FIX dose present in each organ. (Panel B). Dose distribution in the plasma compartment was calculated based on a murine plasma volume of 40 ml/kg body weight. Values are mean +- SEM. Statistical comparisons calculated by t test: *p-value <=0.05, **p-value <=0.005 compared to rFIX WT.

Tissue concentrations and organ distribution of factor IXa variants after tail vein injection in the hemophilia A mouse.

Hemostatic activity of human FIX variants in the saphenous vein bleeding assay.

Wild type (wt) or hemophilia B (KO) C57BL/6J mice were prepped and injected with saline (sham), 0-285 mug/kg FIX WT or rFIX variant via a cannulated jugular vein five minutes prior to vessel injury. Localization of FIX(a) at the injury site.

Schematic depiction of evolving hemostatic response to injury with fibrin clot formation underlying the platelet plug at the injury site. passages.text: Two Cases of Diabetes Remission through Temporary Tirzepatide Treatment

In real-world settings, the incidence of diabetes remission remains low. The factors identified as being associated with diabetes remission included a short duration of diabetes, low baseline hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels, absence of ongoing diabetes pharmacotherapy, and post-intervention weight reduction. However, substantial weight reduction is difficult to achieve in routine clinical practice. Tirzepatide is a novel antidiabetic agent that functions as a dual agonist of the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptors. Clinical trials have shown that tirzepatide significantly reduces HbA1c levels and induces substantial weight reduction. We herein report two cases of diabetes remission after temporary tirzepatide therapy.
Introduction

Type 2 diabetes is a multifactorial disorder characterized by chronic hyperglycemia resulting from both insulin resistance and beta-cell dysfunction and its associated macrovascular and microvascular complications. The disease is progressive, with a gradual decline in the beta-cell function as a common feature. Consequently, blood glucose levels tend to increase with prolonged diabetes, necessitating intensification of therapeutic interventions.

Recently, the concept of "diabetes remission" has gained increasing attention. It is classified into two categories: complete remission, defined as a hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) level of <5.7%, and partial remission, defined as an HbA1c level of <6.5% at least 3 months after cessation of glucose-lowering pharmacotherapy. However, real-world data indicate that the diabetes remission rate is low, with complete and partial remission occurring in only 0.14% and 1.4% of patients, respectively. Previous studies have identified several factors associated with diabetes remission, including a short diabetes duration, low baseline HbA1c levels, absence of current diabetes medication, and body weight (BW) reduction following interventions.

Tirzepatide is a novel anti-diabetic agent that acts as a dual agonist of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptors. Its molecular structure is primarily based on the GIP amino acid sequence and includes a C20 fatty diacid moiety. The Surpass J-mono trial, involving drug-naive Japanese patients with diabetes and an average HbA1c level and body mass index (BMI) of 8.2% and 28 kg/m2, respectively, showed a significant reduction in HbA1c levels by 2.4-2.8% and a BW reduction of 5.8-10.7 kg after tirzepatide treatment for 52 weeks. Although direct evidence regarding the effects of tirzepatide on insulin resistance or the beta-cell function is lacking, histopathological improvements in patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) have been observed following tirzepatide treatment. These findings suggest that tirzepatide may not only improve glycemic control but also exert a beneficial effect on the underlying pathophysiology of type 2 diabetes.
We herein report two cases of diabetes remission after temporary tirzepatide treatment in obese patients with type 2 diabetes and significantly elevated HbA1c levels.
Case Reports
Case 1

A 33-year-old woman was referred to our hospital for the treatment of diabetes. She had been diagnosed with diabetes at a physical checkup one year earlier based on HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose (FPG) levels of 8.1% and 142 mg/dL, respectively. However, the patient did not actually visit hospitals. At a physical examination 1 year later, her HbA1c and FPG levels were 10.4% and 278 mg/dL, respectively, which led to a visit to our hospital and subsequent hospitalization.

Her BW and BMI were 82.7 kg, and 33.1 kg/m2, respectively. No symptoms were observed on admission. The estimated food intake, as determined by dietitians' interviews, was 2,500-2,600 kcal before hospitalization. Blood tests revealed elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (gamma-GTP) levels (Table). A urine examination was negative for ketone bodies and proteins. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed severe fatty liver and visceral fat accumulation (Fig. 1A). The patient received temporary multiple insulin injection therapy with insulin glargine (Gla) and insulin lispro (Lis), in addition to a medical diet of 1,600 kcal/day. Fasting blood glucose (FBG) levels stabilized with the administration of 22 units of Gla and 48 units of Lis, with empagliflozin 10 mg and metformin 2,000 mg. No macro- or micro-complications of diabetes were observed. After the stabilization of blood glucose levels through insulin therapy, the beta-cell function was evaluated. C-peptide levels before and after glucagon loading were 2.45 and 5.42 ng/mL, respectively. The homeostatic model assessment (HOMA2)-%B and HOMA2-%S calculated using FPG and C-peptide levels were 73.9% and 49.9%, respectively. Furthermore, 24-h urine C-peptide excretion was 106 mug/day.
Laboratory Findings of the Two Patients during Hospitalization, after Tirzepatide Treatment, and Six Months after the Discontinuation of Tirzepatide.

To avoid weight gain and hypoglycemia, Lis and Gla were switched to tirzepatide (2.5 mg), and the patient was discharged. Four weeks after discharge, the dosage of tirzepatide was changed to 5.0 mg. Symptomatic hypoglycemia and gastrointestinal-related side effects were not observed.

The clinical course of the patient after discharge is shown in Fig. 2A. After discharge, she was able to maintain a diet of 1,600-1,700 kcal per day. As the patient's HbA1c levels improved and her BW decreased, metformin and empagliflozin were subsequently discontinued. Over the 10 months following her discharge, the patient's HbA1c level remained between 5.3% and 5.5%, with a BW reduction of 16.6 kg with tirzepatide 5.0 mg monotherapy. A blood examination showed improvement in liver dysfunction (Table), and abdominal CT showed marked improvement in fatty liver and visceral fat accumulation (Fig. 1B). Therefore, tirzepatide treatment was discontinued 10 months after discharge. The patient's HbA1c level at 6 months after tirzepatide discontinuation was 5.6% without any medications, and she achieved complete diabetes remission. The HOMA2-%S evaluated after the discontinuation of tirzepatide was improved to 99.4% with a similar HOMA2-%B value of 77.9%.

After the discharge, her HbA1c level showed significant improvement, and metformin and empagliflozin were sequentially discontinued. As tirzepatide monotherapy was able to maintain her HbA1c levels around 5.3% to 5.5%, tirzepatide was also discontinued 10 months after discharge. After the discontinuation of all anti-diabetic agents, the patient's HbA1c levels remained between 5.6% and 5.8%, and diabetes remission was achieved. Her BW decreased by 16.6 kg from discharge to the discontinuation of tirzepatide. After the discontinuation of tirzepatide, her BW remained almost unchanged. B: Course of Case 2. One month after the discharge, the tirzepatide dosage was changed from 2.5 mg to 5.0 mg. As the patient's HbA1c greatly improved, empagliflozin and metformin were discontinued two and four months after his discharge, respectively. As tirzepatide monotherapy was able to maintain his HbA1c levels between 5.6% and 5.7%, tirzepatide was also discontinued 7 months after the discharge. After the discontinuation of all antidiabetic agents, his HbA1c levels remained between 5.8% to 6.1%, and partial diabetes remission was achieved. His BW decreased by 13.0 kg from discharge to the discontinuation of tirzepatide. After the discontinuation of tirzepatide, no marked BW regain was observed.
Case 2

A 49-year-old man was referred to our hospital for diabetes treatment. The patient had been aware of thirst and polyuria for approximately six months. He expressed that his food intake was about 1.5 times the 1,840 kcal diet provided during his hospitalization, but a detailed evaluation could not be performed. His BW and BMI were 83.1 kg, and 29.4 kg/m2, respectively.

The patient's first physical examination in 5 years revealed HbA1c and FPG levels of 12.7% and 260 mg/dL, respectively, and blood tests revealed elevated AST, ALT, and gamma-GTP levels (Table). The urine examination was negative for ketone bodies and proteins. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a fatty liver. The patient was hospitalized and first received a diet of 1,840 kcal per day and temporary multiple insulin injections with Gla and Lis. FBG levels were stabilized by the administration of 15 units of Gla and 31 units of Lis. No macro- or micro-complications of diabetes were observed. His C-peptide levels before and after glucagon loading were 1.79 and 3.89 ng/mL, respectively. However, the glucagon loading test was performed during titration of the basal and bolus insulins. HOMA2-%B and HOMA2-%S evaluated at the same time were 36.7% and 45.4%, respectively. Furthermore, 24-h urine C-peptide excretion after the titration of basal and bolus insulin was 140 mug/day.

After multiple insulin injections for a week, the patient was switched to tirzepatide (2.5 mg), empagliflozin (10 mg), and metformin (1,000 mg) to achieve BW reduction, and the patient was discharged. Fig. 2B shows the clinical course of the patient after discharge. The patient's HbA1c levels improved, and his BW decreased. Because his HbA1c levels improved, empagliflozin and metformin were discontinued two and four months after discharge, respectively. Self-monitoring blood glucose records showed stable FBG levels without hypoglycemia after discharge. No other tirzepatide-induced side effects were observed, including gastrointestinal side effects. Furthermore, because the patient's HbA1c level remained stable at 5.6% with tirzepatide monotherapy and an abdominal ultrasound examination showed improved fatty liver, tirzepatide was discontinued 7 months after discharge. His HbA1c levels remained stable at 5.8-6.1% for 6 months after tirzepatide discontinuation, and he achieved partial diabetes remission. A 75-g glucose tolerance test performed 4 months after tirzepatide discontinuation showed mildly impaired glucose tolerance with FPG and 2-h glucose levels of 107 mg/dL and 143 mg/dL, respectively. HOMA2-%B and HOMA2-%S evaluated 6 months after tirzepatide discontinuation were 104.3% and 94.2%, respectively.
